Against the three gates
All three pre-registered gates fail (Table 1). Gate (a): the argmax-CATE ΔV of +USD 0.20 does not exceed the bootstrap CI width of USD 6.10 — it is smaller by more than an order of magnitude. Gate (b): the DR-learner’s out-of-fold pseudo-outcome R² is −0.25 — the CATE surface fits the cross-fitted pseudo-outcomes worse than their unconditional mean, so it has not learned recoverable heterogeneity. Gate (c): the E-value on the +USD 0.20 improvement is 1.04 (the CI-low maps to the null floor of 1.00), against a 1.25 threshold — an unmeasured confounder with a 1.04× association with both viewing and spending would erase the apparent advantage. The recommendation is to continue send-to-all for the focal offer.


One tension the analysis cannot resolve
A top-K% policy family — treat only the highest-scoring K% — surfaces a signal the argmax-at-threshold policy dilutes. The model-free empirical within-targeted lift (treated minus control spend, among the customers each policy selects) is +USD 149 at top-10% (95% CI [+75, +223]), +USD 110 at top-20% ([+58, +162]), and +USD 77 at top-30% ([+27, +127]) — all with intervals excluding zero, and the top-10% figure reproducing decile 9’s number exactly. The DR policy-value difference for the same policies is null everywhere: −USD 0.03 at top-10%, +USD 10.23 at top-20%, +USD 14.37 at top-30%, all CIs straddling zero (Figure 7).
The two estimators answer different questions. The empirical lift is conditional — “given that the policy selects this customer, what is the treated-minus-control gap?” — and is vulnerable to selection on observables: the customers the model ranks highest may have high baseline spend regardless of viewing. The DR policy value is marginal — “if the policy ran on the whole population, what would average spend be?” — and defaults toward the send-to-all reference when its outcome models cannot fit the top-decile tail. Both mechanisms are operating, and the top-10% empirical interval rests on five control customers, too few to distinguish them. The analysis names the ambiguity rather than resolving it.
Figure 7
The Unresolved Disagreement — Empirical Conditional Lift vs DR Marginal Policy Value

Note. A conditional estimand that excludes zero and a marginal estimand that includes it, on the same policy and the same data.


Sensitivity is uniformly null
The E-value is at the null floor (1.04 point, 1.00 at the CI-low). The propensity-trimming sweep holds ΔV_DR flat between −USD 1.42 and +USD 0.59 across trims from 0% to 20%, every interval crossing zero — the null is not an artefact of any particular overlap region. The seven-variant treatment-window sweep produces a negative pseudo-outcome R² under every definition tested (from −0.13 at a 24-hour view cutoff to −0.64 at 168 hours), including the two variants that achieve genuinely balanced arms and adequate overlap — so the null is not an artefact of the 10-day window or the thin control arm either. And the cross-offer sweep across all 10 catalogue offers finds no offer with a positive ΔV_DR whose CI excludes zero; two offers show the argmax-CATE policy significantly underperforming send-to-all (Figure 8). The focal offer and one sibling discount are sample-constrained (fewer than 200 control customers) at their 96–97% view rates and cannot produce a point estimate at all.
Figure 8
Cross-Offer Applicability Sweep — DR Policy Value vs Send-to-All

Note. Green = adequate overlap; gold = overlap-constrained; red = interval excludes zero (the policy loses). Two offers are omitted as sample-constrained.


The counter-example, preserved
An earlier draft of this analysis defined control as customers who received no offers at all — the naive reading of “untreated”. That group has five customers (three after the training split). On that substrate the same pipeline reports an argmax-CATE policy uplift of +USD 277 (+0.2%) over send-to-all — a number a business would read as a modest positive. It is an identification artefact: with three control customers, the outcome model μ₀ is a near-constant, so the CATE surface is a spend-ranking model that assigns almost every customer a positive score, and the “uplift” is the mechanical consequence. The disciplined analysis and the naive one differ by a control-arm definition; the difference between a defensible null and a confounded positive is entirely in that choice.

title: A CATE-Targeting Policy That Does Not Beat Send-to-All: Five Uplift Estimators, a Three-Gate Decision Rule, and the Diagnostics That Say No
text:
Discussion

The value of the negative result
The pipeline did its job: it produced a pre-registered “no” backed by five estimators, a Qini comparison, a three-gate decision rule, and sensitivity across trimming, treatment definitions, and the whole catalogue — and it exposed the confounded “yes” that a naive control arm would have delivered. False positives in targeting scale linearly in cost across a catalogue of decisions; a single catch of a confounded positive is worth more than a single true positive. The revenue number this study produces is zero, but the deliverable is the discipline for knowing when a CATE-driven policy is ready for a substrate and when it is not.


Why the substrate defeats the method
CATE estimation and policy learning both require overlap — treated and untreated customers at the same covariate values — and the focal offer does not supply it. The 97% view rate is a success of the delivery channel and a failure for causal identification: there is almost no one who received the offer and plausibly could have gone either way on viewing it. Every symptom downstream — the DR-learner’s variance explosion, the negative pseudo-R², the null policy value, the wide bootstrap intervals — traces to that single fact, and the treatment-window sweep confirms it is not fixable by redefining “viewed”.


What would resolve the top-decile tension
The +USD 149 empirical top-decile lift and the DR null are not contradictory; they are a conditional and a marginal estimand disagreeing, with selection-on-observables and outcome-model smoothing both plausible explanations and neither testable at n = 5 controls. A prospective randomised holdout within the top decile resolves it by construction: score a future rollout with the random forest, rank customers, and within the top 10% randomise a small fraction to a no-offer control. Randomisation inside the slice removes the selection interpretation and gives an unbiased estimate the current estimators cannot. At a conservative target effect of +USD 75 (the empirical CI lower bound) against an outcome SD near USD 140, the design needs roughly 45 customers per arm at α = 0.05 one-sided, 80% power — feasible within one observation window.


Limitations
The CATE identification assumption — that age, income, tenure, and pre-period segment block all confounding between viewing and spending — is untestable and, given the overlap diagnostic, weakly supported. The 50-customer test-set control arm makes every interval wide, and the DR-learner’s noise-dominated diagnostics vary at the ±5% level across runs. The segment used for stratification was fit on the full 30-day window; it is leakage-free here only because its features are not post-treatment. The 30-day horizon measures short-run lift per exposure, not lifetime value. And the analysis is single-offer: the cross-offer sweep shows the null generalises across the catalogue’s argmax-at-threshold policies, but the top-decile refinement is specific to the focal offer and would need its own validation.


Conclusion
On the pre-registered decision rule, the CATE targeting policy for the focal offer fails all three gates and the recommendation is to continue send-to-all. The catalogue-wide sweep, the trimming sweep, and the treatment-window sweep all confirm the null. The one live question — whether the top-decile empirical lift is real — cannot be answered observationally at this sample size and is handed forward as a specific, small, feasible randomised test. The infrastructure investments that would lift these constraints are named: a randomised-holdout convention on a fraction of every rollout, and a pre-period capture that would enable variance reduction. The pipeline is the deliverable; the dollar figure is the next study.

title: A Calibrated 30-Day Readmission Model at the Cohort’s Signal Ceiling: Cross-Family Convergence, Isotonic Calibration, and a Fairness Audit
text:
This study builds and validates a supervised model of 30-day hospital readmission for a cohort of 99,340 diabetic inpatient admissions (11.4% readmitted). All estimates come from a held-out test set of 20,031 admissions constructed so that no patient appears in both training and test. Five model families were fitted under a three-tier imbalance ladder — no correction, class weighting with a Youden’s J threshold, and class weighting plus SMOTE — after which the four strongest (LightGBM, XGBoost, CatBoost, and an elastic-net logistic model) were tuned with 50-iteration randomised search under patient-disjoint cross-validation. The tuned models converged to a test ROC-AUC of 0.646–0.668, with the three gradient-boosted families inside a 0.004 band and their predicted probabilities correlated above 0.93; ensemble averaging produced no measurable gain. Class weighting lifted recall from 1.7% to 59% with essentially no change in ranking, and SMOTE degraded performance on every family (−6 to −10 ROC-AUC points for the linear models). Class-weighted probabilities were miscalibrated by construction (Brier 0.21 against a 0.10 null); a single isotonic recalibration restored the base-rate scale (Brier 0.097) while preserving ROC-AUC. On the calibrated probabilities, a broad-screening threshold of 0.15 flags 24.9% of discharges at 46.0% sensitivity, 21.4% precision, and a positive likelihood ratio of 2.1, while flagging the top 1% of risk scores reaches 47% precision. SHAP attributions for LightGBM and XGBoost agreed at a rank correlation of 0.99, with discharge disposition and prior inpatient visits dominating both. A fairness audit across four protected attributes found the largest disparity in payer-code flag rates (2.4× spread, parity ratio 0.42), but within-payer calibration gaps stayed under 2.2 points — the disparity reflects genuine risk heterogeneity, not biased probability estimation. The only structural failure was on the 29 paediatric admissions in the test set, which the adult-trained model never flags.
Keywords: hospital readmission, class imbalance, SMOTE, isotonic calibration, Brier score, SHAP, decision curve analysis, fairness audit, StratifiedGroupKFold

text:
Introduction
Unplanned 30-day readmission is a monitored quality metric and a direct cost to health systems, and diabetic inpatients are among the highest-risk groups. A model that identifies high-risk patients at discharge feeds concrete decisions — transitional-care nurse follow-up, medication reconciliation calls, remote-monitoring enrolment — that are neither free nor unlimited. The model’s job is therefore not to maximise recall but to produce calibrated, explainable, fairness-audited risk estimates that a care-coordination team can act on within its capacity.
Two prior studies of this cohort frame what is achievable. A data-engineering stage produced the analytical table and pre-computed a patient-disjoint cross-validation split. An exploratory analysis showed that the readmission signal is diffuse: no single feature reaches Cohen’s small effect band, prior utilisation carries most of what signal exists, and the published literature reports ROC-AUC ceilings of 0.65–0.70 (Strack et al., 2014). The modelling task is to combine many weak predictors into a defensible score and to characterise its behaviour honestly, not to chase a decimal.
The analysis is organised as a disciplined ladder followed by four validation lenses. The ladder establishes how each algorithm behaves under progressively more aggressive imbalance handling. The lenses — calibration, clinical impact, explainability, and fairness — are the questions a hospital’s algorithmic-review committee would raise, each with a quantitative answer.

title: A Calibrated 30-Day Readmission Model at the Cohort’s Signal Ceiling: Cross-Family Convergence, Isotonic Calibration, and a Fairness Audit
text:
Method

Data and cohort
The source is the Diabetes 130-US Hospitals for Years 1999–2008 dataset (Strack et al., 2014; Clore et al., 2014). The modelling cohort is 99,340 admissions from 69,987 patients, the full extract minus death-or-hospice discharges and invalid-gender records. The binary target, readmission within 30 days, has a positive rate of 11.4% (an imbalance of 7.8:1).


Preprocessing and the patient-disjoint split
Thirty-five of 81 columns were dropped against explicit criteria: the multi-class source readmission label and the fold identifier (target leakage), two string duplicates of integer flags, weight (97% missing), three constant and 13 near-constant medication fields, the nine one-hot primary-diagnosis dummies (replaced by target encoding), and the three raw ICD-9 code columns (replaced by their nine-group aggregations). This left 45 features. Five high-cardinality categoricals (admitting specialty, payer code, three diagnosis groups) were target-encoded on the training fold only; the remaining low-cardinality categoricals were ordinal-encoded with an explicit unknown category.
Because 30% of admissions are repeat visits, the holdout was built with StratifiedGroupKFold (5 splits, random_state = 42) on the patient identifier, taking the first fold’s test partition as a 20% holdout: 79,309 training admissions and 20,031 test admissions, with train and test positive rates of 11.34% and 11.58% and zero patient overlap. The same splitter provided the inner cross-validation during tuning, so patient disjointness holds at every stage.


Model families and the imbalance ladder
Five families were evaluated: plain logistic regression, elastic-net logistic regression, random forest, and the LightGBM and XGBoost gradient-boosted tree libraries (Ke et al., 2017; Chen & Guestrin, 2016). Each was run under three regimes: (1) no imbalance correction at a 0.5 threshold; (2) balanced class weights with the decision threshold set to the point that maximises Youden’s J (Youden, 1950) on the test-set ROC curve; (3) regime 2 plus SMOTE oversampling of the training fold only, inside an imblearn pipeline (Chawla et al., 2002).


Tuning
The three families that separated themselves under class weighting (elastic net, XGBoost, LightGBM), plus CatBoost as a structurally distinct fourth booster (Prokhorenkova et al., 2018), were tuned with 50-iteration RandomizedSearchCV against a 5-fold StratifiedGroupKFold inner CV scored on ROC-AUC, under class weighting and no SMOTE. The elastic-net model was wrapped in a StandardScaler pipeline to stabilise its solver.


Validation lenses
Calibration was assessed with reliability curves and the Brier score (Brier, 1950), and corrected post hoc with isotonic regression fitted on the held-out set (CalibratedClassifierCV(cv="prefit"); Zadrozny & Elkan, 2002). Clinical impact was computed as a threshold grid of sensitivity, specificity, predictive values, likelihood ratios, and number-needed-to-evaluate on the calibrated probabilities, plus a top-K targeting analysis and a decision curve (Vickers & Elkin, 2006). Explainability used SHAP values from TreeExplainer (Lundberg & Lee, 2017; Lundberg et al., 2020) on 2,000 sampled test admissions for LightGBM and XGBoost, compared by rank correlation. Fairness used fairlearn (Bird et al., 2020) to compute per-group selection rate, recall, false-positive rate, and calibration gap across race, gender, age band, and payer code, with the standard note that demographic parity, equalised odds, and calibration cannot jointly hold when base rates differ (Chouldechova, 2017; Kleinberg et al., 2017).


Reproduction
Every number in this article was recomputed from the persisted artefacts — the four tuned estimators, the stored X_test/y_test splits, the SHAP result objects, and the threshold, top-K, calibration, and fairness tables. Training, tuning, and search were not re-run.


Software
Python 3.10 with scikit-learn 1.2, lightgbm, xgboost, catboost, imbalanced-learn, category_encoders, shap, and fairlearn.

title: A Calibrated 30-Day Readmission Model at the Cohort’s Signal Ceiling: Cross-Family Convergence, Isotonic Calibration, and a Fairness Audit
text:
Results

The imbalance ladder: ranking is fixed, recall is a threshold choice
The three regimes moved recall dramatically and left ROC-AUC almost untouched (Figure 1). Under no correction, the best model (LightGBM) reached ROC-AUC 0.667 but caught only 1.7% of true readmissions at the 0.5 threshold — the mathematically correct response to a 7.8:1 imbalance under raw log-loss. Adding balanced class weights and a Youden’s J threshold lifted LightGBM’s recall to 59% at 18% precision, with ROC-AUC essentially unchanged at 0.660. Adding SMOTE on top of that degraded every family: negligibly for LightGBM, by 0.6 points for XGBoost, and by 6.2 and 9.9 points for the two linear models, whose decision boundaries were pulled toward synthetic minority points that do not sit where the real distribution does. Table 1 gives the LightGBM ladder. SMOTE was dropped; class weighting alone carried forward.

The three-tier imbalance ladder across five model families. Left: test ROC-AUC is nearly flat across regimes (SMOTE aside, which collapses the two linear models). Right: recall jumps from near zero to roughly 0.6 once class weights and a Youden’s J threshold are applied.




Four families converge on the same ceiling
Tuned on patient-disjoint folds, LightGBM, XGBoost, and CatBoost reached test ROC-AUCs of 0.668, 0.667, and 0.664 — a spread of 0.004 — with PR-AUCs of 0.226, 0.223, and 0.221 (Figure 2). The elastic-net model trailed at 0.646. LightGBM was selected as primary on PR-AUC (Table 2). The three boosters’ predicted probabilities correlate at 0.94–0.95, so a simple average of them (a Top-2 or Top-3 ensemble) scored 0.668 — identical to LightGBM alone. Four independently tuned algorithms landing within 0.004 of each other is the signal-ceiling result: the limit is the information in the cohort, not the choice of learner.

The three gradient-boosted families converge to a test ROC-AUC band of 0.664–0.668 (shaded); PR-AUC tracks in the 0.22 range. The elastic-net model sits about two points lower on both.




Calibration: class weighting shifts the probability scale
Trained under class weights, all four models produce probabilities on a reweighted 50%-prior scale, not the 11% base rate. Their raw Brier scores (0.21–0.23) are worse than a null model that predicts the base rate for everyone (0.10), and their reliability curves sit far below the diagonal — a raw prediction of 0.40 corresponds to an observed readmission frequency near 0.09 (Figure 3). A single isotonic recalibration, fitted on the held-out set, collapses the Brier score to 0.097–0.099 for every model — below the null baseline — while moving ROC-AUC by at most +0.003. Downstream metrics that depend on the probability value (the threshold grid, the fairness calibration check) use the calibrated model; SHAP uses the raw model, because the isotonic layer is a post-hoc remap, not part of the decision function.



LightGBM reliability on the held-out set. The raw class-weighted curve (Brier 0.212) lies well below the diagonal — systematic over-prediction. Isotonic recalibration (Brier 0.097) pulls it onto the diagonal and back to the 11.6% test base rate.




Clinical impact: the useful threshold is 0.15, not 0.5
On the calibrated LightGBM probabilities, the operating envelope is characterised across the threshold grid (Figure 4). At a 0.15 threshold — a broad-screening operating point — the model flags 24.9% of discharges (4,978 of 20,031), catches 46.0% of readmissions, has a 21.4% positive predictive value, a number-needed-to-evaluate of 4.7, and a positive likelihood ratio of 2.1. That is a resource-reasonable point for a low-cost programme (automated follow-up calls, appointment scheduling). For a high-cost, high-touch intervention, top-K targeting is sharper (Figure 5): flagging the top 1% of risk scores (201 patients) gives a 47% precision and a 4.1× lift over the base rate — 95 of those 201 readmit before a nurse has met them. Precision falls smoothly to 32% at the top 5% and 28% at the top 10%. Table 3 lists the operating points. The four tuned models cluster within one PPV point of each other at any fixed threshold, so the operating-model choice is not a clinical-impact decision.

Explainability: two boosters, one decision logic
SHAP attributions for LightGBM and XGBoost agree almost exactly: a rank correlation of 0.99 across all 45 features and 9 of 10 shared top-ten features (Figure 6). Both put discharge disposition and prior inpatient visits at the top with near-equal weight (mean |SHAP| ≈ 0.22–0.24), then target-encoded admitting specialty (≈ 0.13) and target-encoded primary diagnosis (≈ 0.08). Beyond those four the attribution is spread thinly across length of stay, diagnosis count, payer, and medication counts. The elastic-net model, fitted independently, tells the same story from its coefficients: 32 of 45 features survive its L1 penalty, and the top five — prior inpatient visits (+0.35), discharge disposition (+0.16), admitting specialty (+0.14), the diabetes-medication flag (+0.09), primary diagnosis (+0.07) — carry 52% of the total coefficient mass. All three approaches converge on the same compact clinical picture: a history of admissions, discharged somewhere other than home, treated in a higher-risk service. A 4-to-10-feature score would capture most of the model’s performance.
The HbA1c-testing indicator appears consistently across all three models with a small negative weight (elastic-net coefficient −0.04 at rank 11), suggesting that measuring HbA1c is associated with slightly lower readmission risk. Whether that is a causal effect of testing or a marker of more engaged care is left to a companion causal analysis.



SHAP feature attribution for the primary LightGBM model (left) and its cross-model agreement with XGBoost (right). Discharge disposition and prior inpatient visits dominate; the two boosters’ mean-|SHAP| values fall almost exactly on the identity line (Spearman rank correlation 0.99).




Fairness: one disparity, and it is calibrated
The audit at the 0.15 operating threshold returns a clean four-part finding (Table 4, Figure 7).
Gender shows no meaningful disparity — a demographic-parity ratio of 0.91 and a recall gap of 3.4 points, tracking a genuine base-rate difference between female and male patients.
Race shows an apparent disparity in the headline numbers (parity ratio 0.53) that is entirely an artefact of the four smallest groups (each 135–449 test patients). Restricted to the two large groups (Caucasian and African American, 94% of the test cohort), the flag-rate gap is 2.7 points and the recall gap 3.8 points — small and coherent.
Age shows a real structural failure, but not a bias: the 29 paediatric ([0–10)) admissions in the test set are never flagged (zero flag rate, zero recall). The adult-trained decision function produces probabilities for these patients that fall below any usable threshold. This is a scope problem — paediatric readmission has different drivers — and the recommendation is to route paediatric discharges to a separate workflow. Adult age bands perform comparably (recall 0.44–0.49 for every band above 500 patients).
Payer code shows the largest disparity: flag rates range from 12% to 28% across payer groups, a 2.4× spread and a parity ratio of 0.42, well below the 0.80 convention. But the actual readmission rates track the flag rates — Medicare patients are flagged at 28% and readmit at 12.8%; Blue Cross patients are flagged at 14% and readmit at 7.6% — and within-payer calibration gaps stay under 2.2 points for every group. The model is not mis-estimating risk for any payer; it is correctly reporting that patients on different plans carry different baseline risk. The recommendation is to deploy with ongoing monitoring of the payer disparity and explicit documentation, not to suppress it.

title: A Calibrated 30-Day Readmission Model at the Cohort’s Signal Ceiling: Cross-Family Convergence, Isotonic Calibration, and a Fairness Audit
text:
Discussion
Principal findings. A tuned gradient-boosted model reaches a held-out ROC-AUC of 0.67 on this cohort, and four independent model families agree to within 0.004 — the ceiling is the data. Class weighting converts the ranking into a usable decision by lifting recall from 2% to 59%; SMOTE adds nothing and harms linear models. The class-weighted probabilities need one isotonic step to be interpretable as probabilities. On the calibrated scale, a 0.15 threshold is a reasonable broad-screen and top-1% targeting is a strong precision play. The model’s decision logic is compact, clinically sensible, and identical across two boosters and a linear model.
The mechanism is that the top features are markers of instability at discharge, not causes of readmission. Discharge disposition, prior inpatient visits, and admitting specialty all encode the same latent quantity — how sick and how unstable the patient was when they left. The model predicts that latent state; it does not point at an intervention. That is why the downstream work is a targeting-and-intervention design, not a lever-finding exercise.
Limitations. This is a single train/test split on a historical cohort (1999–2008); no external validation was performed. The isotonic calibrator, the Youden threshold, and the fairness metrics were all computed on the same held-out set, so they carry a mild optimism — the honest headline is the tuned ROC-AUC of 0.67, which the model never saw during training or tuning. Target encoding was fitted on the training fold, but the calibrator’s use of test labels means the reported Brier and operating-point numbers are best read as upper bounds on deployed performance. The paediatric subgroup is too small to model; the smallest racial and payer subgroups have unstable rate estimates. Discharge disposition is available at discharge, which is the intended prediction time, but a hospital deploying earlier in the stay would lose the single strongest feature.
Conclusion. The cohort supports a calibrated, explainable readmission-risk model with a well-understood operating envelope and one documented fairness caveat that resolves on inspection. The reported ROC-AUC of 0.67 is the honest figure; the operating-point metrics are diagnostics on the same split and should be revalidated before deployment.

title: An Operator-Truth-Preserving Medallion ETL Pipeline for a City Part 1 Crime Archive
text:
This is the extract–transform–load (ETL) stage of a six-notebook project on eleven years of urban crime. It has one job: turn a raw municipal open-data export — 546,800 incident records in a GeoJSON file, plus a 203-row crime-code lookup and two spatial-enrichment assets — into an analysis-ready set of Parquet tables that the exploratory, modelling, fairness, clustering, and regression notebooks each load without re-running any upstream logic. The dataset is a large U.S. city’s Part 1 file: the serious “index” offences — homicide, rape, robbery, aggravated assault, burglary, larceny, auto theft, and arson — reported between 2012 and 2022. The city is not named here; the interest is in the pipeline, not the jurisdiction.
The pipeline follows a four-tier medallion architecture (Raw → Bronze → Silver → Gold), where each tier has a strict contract, a distinct fault-isolation boundary, and a persisted Parquet snapshot any consumer can reload independently. The finding that shapes every design decision is that this data was entered by people, under time pressure, into a constrained form — and the resulting artefacts are not random noise. A Weapon value of NA is not a missing value; it is an operator’s affirmative statement that no weapon was involved, and it is the single largest token in the column. A Gender value of U is a deliberate “I don’t know,” which is analytically different from the string 042819 that a fat-fingered entry produced. An Inside_Outside value of None was picked from a menu. The pipeline’s central principle is to preserve these operator-entered distinctions as explicit, named categories rather than collapsing them into a single null — because collapsing them silently destroys real signal, and in the weapon column that signal covers 69% of the cohort.

title: An Operator-Truth-Preserving Medallion ETL Pipeline for a City Part 1 Crime Archive
text:
Pipeline architecture
Each tier knows strictly more about the data than the one before it. Raw knows nothing — it is a byte-for-byte snapshot. Bronze knows what the data looks like — column names, key fragments, dtypes. Silver knows what the data means — sentinels, controlled vocabularies, coordinate validity, the temporal window. Gold produces the analytical surface — spatial enrichment, the Part 1 filter, weapon unification, dimensional modelling, and 13 pre-computed features. The contract for each tier — and, just as important, what each tier must not do — is fixed (Figure 1, Table 1).

title: An Operator-Truth-Preserving Medallion ETL Pipeline for a City Part 1 Crime Archive
text:
Raw ingestion and audit
The GeoJSON source loads as a 546,800 × 22 GeoDataFrame; the crime-code lookup as 203 × 8. Both are snapshotted to Parquet before any transformation as the lineage anchor — if a downstream finding is ever challenged, the exact source state at run time can be reloaded without re-parsing the 322 MB GeoJSON. The audit that follows reads the untouched frame, names every structural and distributional problem, and establishes the evidence for each later transformation.

Structural artefacts
All 21 attribute columns carry mixed casing; two names fragment incorrectly under naive snake_case conversion (RowID → row_i_d, VRIName → v_r_i_name). The first is the join key for the Gold spatial-enrichment step, so its correct repair is a hard dependency. CrimeDateTime arrives as an object string with 359,213 distinct values — every temporal feature and both derived key columns depend on Silver’s UTC-aware parse. Two columns are inert: Total_Incidents is a constant 1 (a row-counter vestige), and Shape is 100% null (a geometry-metadata artefact). Both are carried to Gold and dropped there.


The missingness surface
Missingness is severe and structurally uneven (Figure 2). Ethnicity is absent on 96.5% of rows and VRIName on 88.4% — these are collection gaps, not pipeline faults, and the downstream notebooks treat their missingness rates as hard analytical constraints. Age (20.2%), Gender (16.2%), Premise (13.9%), and Inside_Outside (13.8%) sit in a middle band. Every structural field — the coordinate pair, Location, Neighborhood, District, Post — is missing on well under 1% of rows. The 900 rows (0.16%) with an identical missing count across Latitude, Longitude, and geometry are the same records: the bad-geocoding placeholder pairs the source writes as (0.0, 0.0) and the string (,).
Figure 2
The Raw Missingness Landscape, and Its Resolution

Note. Amber = demographic or descriptive field; grey = structural field. Silver and Gold resolve every gap either by an explicit token (Unknown, Unsure, Not Applicable) or, for age alone, by mean imputation — the one imputation the pipeline performs, made at Silver because every downstream consumer uses age as a continuous feature and a single consistent fill is preferable to five notebooks each choosing their own.


Vocabulary fragmentation
Gender carries 31 distinct non-null tokens; Weapon carries 24; Inside_Outside carries four tokens spanning two logical states. The unique-value counts understate the problem — the fragmentation is a mix of abbreviation variants, operator-asserted uncertainty tokens, and uninterpretable entries that need three qualitatively different treatments. Figures 3 and 4 make the two consequential cases concrete.

text:
Bronze layer — structural cleaning
Bronze applies snake_case normalisation and two targeted fragment repairs, then asserts that row_id is present. No value is changed, no row is filtered, no column is added or removed. Shape is unchanged at 546,800 × 22; the Parquet file writes at 36.5 MB (down from a 535 MB in-memory footprint) under Snappy compression. Bronze is the reload point for any issue that traces to column naming, key-fragment repair, or join-key presence.

text:
Silver layer — business-logic cleaning
Silver resolves each finding from the raw audit through an explicit, documented rule. The vocabulary work is where the operator-truth principle first bites (Table 2).

Note. The gender split is the pattern: the operator’s deliberate “I don’t know” (U, 11,943 raw rows) is analytically different from a value the system cannot interpret, so the two are kept in separate buckets. Collapsing them would inflate the “unknown” count with a small but real population of data-entry noise.
Figure 3 shows the gender collapse. The two canonical abbreviations account for 95% of non-null entries; the operator-asserted Unknown is a visible middle band; the entire uninterpretable tail is 183 rows across 22 token types.
Figure 3
31 Raw Gender Tokens Collapse to Five States

Note. Agender exists in the mapping for forward compatibility but no row in this eleven-year extract maps to it.
Coordinates and time. The enforce_bounding_box helper nulls latitude and longitude together for any pair where either component falls outside the city rectangle — a partially valid pair is as unusable spatially as a fully wrong one. This lifts the coordinate null count from 900 to 978 (the extra 78 are pairs that parsed cleanly but land outside the city). crime_date_time is parsed UTC-aware; rows outside the 2012–2022 operational window are removed. This is the single largest row loss in the pipeline: 49,127 pre-2012 timestamps (legacy-system contamination) plus 2 unparseable values, for 49,129 rows. Silver output: 497,671 × 25.
The crime-code lookup. Silver proper-cases the labels, renames the opaque source columns, and filters crime_class == "PART 1" — reducing the lookup from 203 to 88 rows. This filter defines the analytical cohort: the Gold inner join on crime_code will exclude any fact row whose code is not among these 88. A derived crime_category field maps the fine-grained subcategory strings to the eight canonical buckets (39 of the 88 codes are Robbery variants; 17 are Arson; the rest spread across the other six).

title: An Operator-Truth-Preserving Medallion ETL Pipeline for a City Part 1 Crime Archive
section: Gold layer — the analytical fact grain
text:
Gold layer — the analytical fact grain
Gold operates on Silver inputs only and applies five things in sequence.
Spatial enrichment. Two geocoding assets from a prior mapping-API pass are coalesced into the frame with combine_first, filling only where Silver’s value was NaN — a valid Silver coordinate is never overwritten. The bounding box is re-enforced (geocoders occasionally return out-of-city points), then rows with fewer than three of the five key location fields populated are dropped: 497,671 → 497,342, a loss of 329.
The Part 1 join. An inner join on crime_code against the 88-row dimension brings the cohort to its final size: 497,342 → 407,826, excluding 89,516 rows whose codes are Part 2 misdemeanours, calls-for-service, or administrative entries. Deduplication on row_id finds zero duplicates — the join produced no fan-out. Figure 5 is the complete row ledger.
Figure 5
Cohort Row Accounting — Every Dropped Record Attributed

Note. 546,800 − 49,129 − 329 − 89,516 = 407,826. No other step removes a row.
Operator-truth weapon unification. Two standardisers run before a combine_first merge. The fact-side function preserves NA → Not Applicable and UNKNOWN → Unknown as terminal sentinels while routing genuine blanks to NaN; the dimension-side function — working from a coarse four-token fallback taxonomy that carries no operator-truth distinctions — routes everything null-flavoured to NaN. The fact signal wins where it exists; any residual NaN becomes Unknown. The result (Figure 4): Not Applicable is 281,645 incidents — 69.06% of the cohort — and it is a first-class category, never folded into the 20,049-row Unknown bucket or into a null.
Figure 4
The Unified Weapon Vocabulary — ‘Not Applicable’ Is a Category, Not a Gap

Note. Any weapon analysis in the downstream notebooks must treat Not Applicable and Unknown as separate categories; a single “missing weapon” bucket would merge an affirmative signal with an absence of one.

title: An Operator-Truth-Preserving Medallion ETL Pipeline for a City Part 1 Crime Archive
text:
Dimensions and the consolidated fact
Twelve dimension tables wrap the fact grain (Figure 6). Ten are thin drop_duplicates constructions with a 1-indexed surrogate key; dim_crime_codes is a Silver pass-through; dim_date (3,997 rows, one per calendar date) and dim_time (1,440 rows, one per minute of the day) carry pre-computed calendar and clock attributes. The consolidated fact_crimes_gold merges every dimension’s surrogate key back onto the enriched rows, assigns its own crime_event_id primary key, and drops the descriptive columns and the two free-form text fields (address, location). Result: 407,826 × 35, integer-keyed, with zero missing surrogate keys across all 12 key columns — no join in the chain relies on NaN == NaN.

title: An Operator-Truth-Preserving Medallion ETL Pipeline for a City Part 1 Crime Archive
text:
Carry-forward findings
Five facts the downstream notebooks inherit and must account for.

The cohort is fully geocoded. HasValidCoordinates is uniformly True across all 407,826 rows; spatial analyses can treat the coordinate pair as complete without a pre-filter. The final composition is 63.7% property crime (259,660) and 36.3% violent crime (148,166), across eight categories from Larceny (175,484) down to Arson (2,158) — the class balance that the binary-classification notebook works from (Figure 7).
weapon_unified has two operator-truth tokens. Not Applicable (281,645; 69.1%) and Unknown (20,049; 4.9%) are distinct categories. Any weapon analysis that merges them merges an affirmative “no weapon” with an absence of information.
district and neighbourhood carry an explicit Unknown member. 1,452 and 1,483 rows respectively resolve to it. Spatial aggregations produce an Unknown group that should be acknowledged, not silently dropped.
ethnicity is 96.5% Unknown and vri_name 88.4% missing. These are collection gaps. ethnicity cannot support a stratification analysis; treat its missingness rate as a hard ceiling on what the column can do.
age is the only imputed column. Its residual nulls were mean-filled at Silver. Models that lean on age should carry a note that a minority of values are imputed, not observed.

title: Health Analytics & Biostatistics — Exploratory Analysis of a Diabetic Inpatient Cohort
text:
This notebook is the second checkpoint in the diabetes-readmission portfolio. The first checkpoint (00_etl_diabetes.ipynb) closed with three Gold-layer feature tables — hospital_admissions_gold (101,766 rows), modelling_cohort_gold (99,340 rows after terminal-discharge and gender exclusions), and hba1c_cohort_gold (one row per patient, 69,987 patients) — plus three dimension lookups and the patient-level five-fold CV assignment. This notebook reads those Gold tables back in and runs the full exploratory and statistical analysis on top.
The arc has twelve sections. Sections 2–4 profile the cohort along three lenses — population (demographics), clinical picture (diagnoses, length of stay, prior utilisation), and medications. Sections 5–7 introduce the readmission target and run the bivariate signal scans (continuous in §6, categorical in §7). Sections 8–9 switch to the HbA1c testing landscape, fit a propensity-score logistic regression to surface the strongest confounders, and quantify the naive treatment effect with a stratified preview that motivates the causal analysis in notebook 03. Sections 10–11 close the modelling-readiness loop: a multicollinearity scan over the continuous feature set, then a five-check verification of the patient-level CV folds (per-fold rate, patient-disjoint integrity, feature stability, and two empirical leakage probes). Section 12 wraps with three concrete modelling hypotheses for notebook 02 and the causal question for notebook 03.
A note on house style. Every concrete number cited in the prose is anchored in a printed output further down in the cell or in an immediately-adjacent code cell — no visual reads. The plotting helpers used throughout (pl.plot_categorical, pl.plot_target_rate_by_category, pl.plot_target_rate_by_quantile, pl.plot_stratified_rate, pl.plot_box_categorical, pl.plot_numeric_dist) all print compact summary tables under their charts via show_summary=True, so every claim about a count, a rate, a quantile, or a stratum-level difference traces directly to numerical output the reader can verify.

1 · Setup, Load, Audit
The setup cell below imports the standard data-science stack (pandas, numpy, scipy, statsmodels, matplotlib, seaborn) plus my reusable python_scripts package (aliased as ps). title: Health Analytics & Biostatistics — Exploratory Analysis of a Diabetic Inpatient Cohort
text:
2 · The Patient Population
Before asking which patients readmit, I need to understand who the patients are. This section profiles the demographic side of the cohort: age band, gender, race, payer mix, and admitting specialty. Each subsection produces a single distributional plot — counts and percentages for the categorical features — and the section closes with a Cramér’s V matrix that quantifies how strongly the demographic features associate with each other.
The point is not to test demographic features against the readmission target yet — that work happens in §5, where the target enters formally and every covariate gets its own readmission-rate breakdown. What I am doing here is establishing the population baseline, so that when §5 reports a per-age-band or per-payer readmission rate, the reader already knows what proportion of the cohort sits in each bucket. A 14% readmission rate in a band that holds 1.7% of the cohort means something very different from a 14% rate in a band that holds 22%.
The demographic profile also feeds two analytical decisions later. First, the strongest demographic association in the Cramér’s V matrix tells me which pairs of features will create multicollinearity in the multivariate phase — that ends up mattering for the propensity model in §8 and the multicollinearity scan in §10. Second, the share of admissions concentrated in high-cardinality categorical features (medical specialty in particular) tells the modelling notebook how aggressively to encode them.

2.1 Age distribution
The dataset bins age into ten-year intervals — [0-10) through [90-100) — exactly as it ships from the source. I keep the binning at the EDA stage rather than collapsing or re-binning, because the bands are clinically meaningful (paediatric, working-age, geriatric) and any re-binning would obscure where the cohort’s mass actually sits.
The chart below plots the count of admissions in each band as a horizontal bar, and the printed Category Summary directly underneath gives the exact count and percentage for each band.


📊 Category Summary

column: age | total_n: 99,340 | n_unique: 10 | displayed: 10 | hidden: 0 | displayed_share_%: 100.00

category: [70-80) | count: 25329 | pct_of_total: 25.50 | 

category: [60-70) | count: 22058 | pct_of_total: 22.20 | 

category: [50-60) | count: 17060 | pct_of_total: 17.17 | 

category: [80-90) | count: 16434 | pct_of_total: 16.54 | 

category: [40-50) | count: 9607 | pct_of_total: 9.67 | 

category: [30-40) | count: 3764 | pct_of_total: 3.79 | 

category: [90-100) | count: 2589 | pct_of_total: 2.61 | 

category: [20-30) | count: 1649 | pct_of_total: 1.66 | 

category: [10-20) | count: 690 | pct_of_total: 0.69 | 

category: [0-10) | count: 160 | pct_of_total: 0.16 |
The cohort is heavily weighted toward older adults, exactly as one would expect of a diabetic-inpatient population in the United States. The [70-80) band is the modal bucket at 25.50% (25,329 admissions), followed by [60-70) at 22.20% (22,058) and [80-90) at 16.54% (16,434). The three senior bands together — [60-70), [70-80), [80-90) — cover 64.0% of the cohort, and the full geriatric range from age 60 upward (adding [90-100) at 2.61%) covers 66.9%.
The non-senior tail thins out predictably. [50-60) is meaningful at 17.17% (17,060 admissions), and [40-50) holds 9.67% (9,607). Below age 40 the cohort gets thin: [30-40) at 3.79%, [20-30) at 1.66% (1,649), [10-20) at 0.69% (690), and [0-10) at 0.16% (160). The two youngest bands together hold fewer than 850 admissions and any per-band statistic computed on them carries wide confidence intervals — I’ll be careful to flag this when these bands reappear in §5.2.
Two analytical implications fall out. First, age is going to be a real predictor of readmission downstream — but the demographic centre of gravity is already in the at-risk geriatric range, so the differentiation will come from contrasts within the senior bands rather than between seniors and the under-40 tail. §5.2 will test that empirically. Second, my engineered age_midpoint_squared feature is justified by this distribution: a linear-only age term would force a model to fit a straight line through a distribution whose centre of mass sits in a narrow age band, and the quadratic gives the linear models the curvature they need. Tree models will use the linear term and ignore the quadratic; linear models will use both.


2.2 Gender distribution
The dataset records three gender categories: Male, Female, and Unknown/Invalid. The third category contains only three rows in the full admission table, and notebook 00’s modelling-cohort builder dropped them as part of the cohort exclusions, so the version of the data I’m looking at here holds two values only.


📊 Category Summary

column: gender | total_n: 99,340 | n_unique: 2 | displayed: 2 | hidden: 0 | displayed_share_%: 100.00

category: Female | count: 53454 | pct_of_total: 53.81 | 

category: Male | count: 45886 | pct_of_total: 46.19 |
The split is Female 53.81% (53,454 admissions) and Male 46.19% (45,886) — slightly female-skewed but close enough to balanced that no analytical decision in this notebook depends on the imbalance. The skew is consistent with what one would expect from an older-skewed inpatient cohort in the United States: women live longer than men on average, and the [70-80), [80-90), and [90-100) age bands that dominate this dataset are exactly where the female-to-male ratio in the general population starts to widen. The gender skew here is a demographic consequence of the age distribution above, not an independent recruitment bias in the data.
Two implications. First, gender will enter the modelling notebook as a binary feature without any need for re-balancing. Second, when §5.6 looks at readmission rate by gender, any difference between the two arms will be measured against an honest denominator — each arm carries enough rows (~54k female, ~46k male) that confidence intervals on per-arm rates will be tight, and any meaningful difference will surface clearly rather than being lost in sampling noise.
`### 2.3 Race distribution
Race in the source data is recorded as one of five categories — Caucasian, AfricanAmerican, Hispanic, Asian, Other — with a small share of admissions missing the field. Notebook 00’s Silver layer left the categorical structure intact and the missing values as pd.NA; Gold’s _sanitize_gold_strings then converted them to the literal string "Missing" so downstream models can handle them without falling into NaN-comparison semantics.
A note on framing. Race in this dataset is a recorded category rather than a clinical mechanism. Any association between race and readmission that this notebook surfaces will be a correlation — most likely with confounding through socioeconomic factors, healthcare access, comorbidity profile, and admitting specialty patterns rather than through any direct biological pathway.


📊 Category Summary

column: race | total_n: 99,340 | n_unique: 6 | displayed: 6 | hidden: 0 | displayed_share_%: 100.00

category: Caucasian | count: 74220 | pct_of_total: 74.71 | 

category: AfricanAmerican | count: 18772 | pct_of_total: 18.90 | 

category: Missing | count: 2232 | pct_of_total: 2.25 | 

category: Hispanic | count: 2017 | pct_of_total: 2.03 | 

category: Other | count: 1471 | pct_of_total: 1.48 | 

category: Asian | count: 628 | pct_of_total: 0.63 |
The distribution is heavily skewed toward two majority categories. Caucasian patients account for 74.71% of admissions (74,220) and AfricanAmerican patients for 18.90% (18,772) — together those two cover 93.61% of the cohort. The remaining four categories sit in the long tail: Missing at 2.25% (2,232), Hispanic at 2.03% (2,017), Other at 1.48% (1,471), and Asian at 0.63% (628).
The skew has direct analytical consequences. Any per-race readmission rate the notebook reports later will carry tight confidence intervals for the two majority categories and meaningfully wider intervals for Hispanic, Other, Missing, and Asian — small differences in those four will not pass formal significance even when they look interesting on a bar chart. The chi-square test in the next cell takes this honestly: it tests whether the joint distribution of race and readmission departs from independence anywhere across all six categories.
The roughly 75-to-19 Caucasian-to-AfricanAmerican ratio is also relevant to the planned fairness audit in notebook 02. The audit will measure how the predictive model performs across protected groups including race; the heavy concentration in two categories means the audit will have plenty of statistical power for the Caucasian-vs-AfricanAmerican comparison and progressively less for the smaller groups.
A first formal test: is race independent of 30-day readmission, or are the rates meaningfully different across groups?
Chi-square test of independence: race × readmitted_30d
============================================================
  H₀ : race and readmitted_30d are independent
  H₁ : race and readmitted_30d are associated
  α  : 0.05
------------------------------------------------------------
  Chi² statistic               =       26.884
  Degrees of freedom           = 5
  p-value                      = 0.0001
  Cramér's V (bias-corrected)  = 0.0148

  Effect size — Cohen's conventions for Cramér's V (dof = 1)
     negligible: V < 0.10  |  small: 0.10–0.20  |  moderate: 0.20–0.40  |  large: V ≥ 0.40
     → observed V = 0.0148 → negligible
------------------------------------------------------------
  Decision : REJECT H₀ at α = 0.05  (p = 0.0001 < 0.05)
  Reading  : The two variables are statistically associated, but the
             effect size is negligible — meaningful significance, not
             necessarily meaningful magnitude.

Readmission rate by race (%):
race
AfricanAmerican    11.45
Asian              10.35
Caucasian          11.53
Hispanic           10.51
Missing             8.42
Other               9.79
The chi-square test is statistically significant — χ² = 26.88 on 5 degrees of freedom, p = 0.0001 — and the null hypothesis of independence between race and 30-day readmission is rejected. But the effect size is Cramér’s V = 0.0148, which by Cohen’s conventions for chi-square effect sizes (negligible < 0.10, small 0.10–0.20, moderate 0.20–0.40, large > 0.50) classes as negligible. The per-race readmission rates the test produces (printed at the bottom of the test output above) are tightly clustered: Caucasian 11.53%, AfricanAmerican 11.45%, Hispanic 10.51%, Asian 10.35%, Other 9.79%, Missing 8.42%. The spread between highest and lowest non-missing categories is around 1.8 percentage points.
This is the classic large-N paradox: with 99,340 admissions, the chi-square test has enormous statistical power, and even a vanishingly small departure from independence becomes statistically detectable. The p-value alone tells me nothing useful about whether the association matters; the effect size does.
The reading I take forward is: race and readmission are not independent, but the association is too weak to act as a primary driver of the modelling pipeline. Any predictive value race carries will most likely come through interactions and confounding rather than through a direct main effect, and the modelling notebook will encode race as one of several demographic features without any special treatment. The negligible effect size also informs how I’ll read the fairness audit in notebook 02: a model that produces meaningfully different performance across racial groups would be doing so primarily because race correlates with other features (insurance, comorbidity profile, admitting specialty) rather than because the cohort base rates differ sharply by race.
This is also a useful illustration of the p-value vs effect size distinction that runs through the rest of this notebook: with ~99k rows, statistical significance is cheap, so I lean on effect-size measures (Cramér’s V, point-biserial r, rank-biserial r) to judge what is actually informative.


2.4 Payer mix
Payer code records the patient’s primary payer at admission — Medicare, Medicaid, private insurance carriers, self-pay, and so on. The full admission table holds 17 distinct payer codes plus the engineered Missing category, with around 40% of admissions missing the field. Missingness at this scale is itself meaningful: it almost certainly reflects hospitals where the payer code was not reliably captured at intake rather than admissions where no payer existed, and the modelling notebook will treat Missing as its own category rather than imputing.
The chart below is a Pareto plot — payer codes ranked left-to-right by admission count, with a cumulative-share curve overlaid. The Pareto framing is appropriate because payer mix tends to follow a power law, with a small number of dominant payers covering the bulk of admissions and a long tail of smaller payers contributing fractions of a percent each. The cumulative curve makes it easy to see how many payer codes are needed to cover, say, 80% of the active-payer mass, which informs the high-cardinality encoding strategy in notebook 02.
I drop the missing-payer rows from this plot for visual clarity — the goal is to see the shape of the active payer distribution, not to compete with the missingness bar. The missingness rate is reported separately (the modelling cohort has 39.66% missing, ~39,397 admissions) and accounted for in the modelling pipeline.

The Pareto chart confirms the expected power-law shape. Medicare (MC) dominates the active-payer distribution at 31,333 admissions — 31.54% of the full cohort and 52.3% of the non-missing payer codes (since 39.66% of the cohort is in the Missing bucket). HM (the dominant private/HMO carrier in this dataset) follows at 6,195 admissions (6.24% of the cohort), with SP (self-pay), BC (Blue Cross), and MD (Medicaid) rounding out the top five at 4,941, 4,601, and 3,473 admissions respectively. The top five non-missing payer codes together cover 84.3% of the non-missing mass.
Two analytical implications. First, the Medicare dominance is itself a demographic statement: Medicare is the primary US payer for patients aged 65 and over, and its dominance here echoes the heavy senior skew the age distribution showed in §2.1. The Cramér’s V matrix at the close of this section will quantify the strength of that age-payer association directly — and it does come back as the second-strongest demographic pair. Second, the heavy concentration in the top few payer codes tells the modelling notebook that target encoding is the right choice for this column: one-hot encoding 17 levels would explode the feature space unnecessarily, and target encoding will collapse the long tail into a single numeric value per code that captures the per-payer base rate without the dimensionality cost.
The high missingness rate (~40%) deserves one more comment. A model trained on a cohort where missing-payer is a category in its own right will learn whatever signal that category carries — and depending on which hospitals or admission types tend to leave the field blank, that signal may be substantial. §5 will check whether the Missing category has a different readmission rate from the recorded categories.


2.5 Top admitting specialties
Medical specialty records the specialty of the admitting physician — internal medicine, cardiology, family practice, and so on. This is the highest-cardinality categorical feature in the cohort: the column holds 73 distinct values including the engineered Missing category, and around 49% of admissions have it missing. The missingness rate roughly halves the effective coverage and will need a Missing category rather than imputation, exactly as in the payer-code case above.
The chart below shows the top 15 admitting specialties by admission count. I cap the display at 15 because the long tail extends well beyond that — the bottom ~58 specialties together account for under 5% of admissions and would crowd the chart without adding analytical signal. The printed Category Summary directly under the chart prints the exact counts plus the displayed_share_% field that quantifies how much of the cohort the top-15 actually covers.
The cardinality and the missingness rate together tell me everything I need to know about how this column will enter the modelling pipeline. Target encoding is the right move for notebook 02 — converting each specialty to its per-specialty readmission rate gives the model a single numeric value per category that compresses 73 levels into one feature, and the rare-category problem (specialties with fewer than ~30 admissions) gets handled smoothly because the encoder can fall back on a smoothed prior.


📊 Category Summary

column: medical_specialty | total_n: 99,340 | n_unique: 73 | displayed: 15 | hidden: 58 | displayed_share_%: 95.47

category: Missing | count: 48614 | pct_of_total: 48.94 | 

category: InternalMedicine | count: 14237 | pct_of_total: 14.33 |

The top-15 displayed specialties cover 95.47% of the cohort, leaving the bottom 58 specialties with under 5% of mass between them — clean Pareto behaviour. The largest single category is Missing at 48,614 admissions (48.94%) — the missingness rate dominates the column. Among the recorded specialties, InternalMedicine is the largest at 14,237 admissions (14.33%), unsurprising for a diabetic inpatient cohort where diabetic complications are most often handled on internal-medicine wards. Emergency/Trauma at 7,419 (7.47%), Family/GeneralPractice at 7,252 (7.30%), and Cardiology at 5,278 (5.31%) round out the top four.
Two analytical threads pick up later. First, the 48.94% missingness rate in this column means that nearly half the cohort will land in the Missing specialty bucket, and the modelling notebook needs to test whether that bucket carries its own readmission-rate signal. Second, Cardiology appearing in the top four is consistent with the Circulatory primary-diagnosis dominance I’ll show in §3.1 — many of these admissions are diabetic patients admitted for cardiovascular events, with diabetes as a comorbidity rather than primary condition. That cross-feature association is exactly what the Cramér’s V matrix in the next subsection is designed to surface.


2.6 Demographic association matrix
To close the demographic profile, I check whether the five demographic features — age, gender, race, payer code, and admitting specialty — carry overlapping information. A high Cramér’s V between two of them would mean the second feature is largely redundant once the first is in the model, which has implications for the multicollinearity scan in §10 and the propensity-score covariate set in §8.
The chart below renders a Cramér’s V matrix as a heatmap, with the off-diagonal values printed inside each cell. Cramér’s V here is bias-corrected (Bergsma 2013) so that the values are comparable across pairs with different cardinalities — the unadjusted version is biased upward when one of the variables has many levels, which would distort the comparison between, say, gender × age (2 × 10 levels) and medical_specialty × payer_code (~73 × 18 levels). Below the heatmap, a ranked summary table prints the ten strongest pairs in descending order, with Cohen’s interpretation bands attached.


📊 Cramér's V — pairwise summary (bias-corrected, ranked)
======================================================================
  Cohen's conventions for Cramér's V (dof = 1):
     negligible: V < 0.10  |  small: 0.10–0.20
     moderate:   0.20–0.40 |  large: V ≥ 0.40
----------------------------------------------------------------------
     feature_a          feature_b  cramers_v
1          age  medical_specialty     0.2524
2          age         payer_code     0.1536
3       gender  medical_specialty     0.1151
4          age             gender     0.1117
5   payer_code  medical_specialty     0.1085
6         race  medical_specialty     0.0941
7         race         payer_code     0.0870
8          age               race     0.0847
9       gender         payer_code     0.0841
10      gender               race     0.0706
The matrix is mostly quiet. The strongest pair is age × medical_specialty at V = 0.252, which lands in the moderate band — older patients are systematically routed to different admitting specialties than younger ones (geriatrics, cardiology, internal medicine for the senior bands; paediatric subspecialties for the very young; obstetrics-related specialties for working-age women). This is mechanical rather than informational, but it is strong enough that the propensity model in §8 will need to handle the pair carefully — if both age and medical specialty enter the covariate set together, the coefficient on each will absorb part of what the other could explain.
The next-strongest pair is age × payer_code at V = 0.154 (small) — Medicare eligibility kicks in at 65, so patients in the senior age bands are mechanically more likely to carry Medicare as their primary payer. This is again a structural rather than analytical association, and again worth flagging for the propensity model’s covariate handling.
Below those two, the rest of the matrix sits in the small-to-negligible range: gender × medical_specialty at V = 0.115, age × gender at V = 0.112, payer_code × medical_specialty at V = 0.109, race × medical_specialty at V = 0.094, race × payer_code at V = 0.087, age × race at V = 0.085, gender × payer_code at V = 0.084, and gender × race at V = 0.071. None of those pairs warrants special handling.
The two real findings — the moderate age-specialty association and the small age-payer association — are both expected given how US healthcare routes patients by age, and both will be visible in the multicollinearity scan in §10 when the engineered prior_visits_x_age interaction term shows up alongside the linear age term. With the demographic landscape mapped, I move to the clinical features.

title: Health Analytics & Biostatistics — Exploratory Analysis of a Diabetic Inpatient Cohort
text:
3 · The Clinical Picture
This section profiles the clinical features of each admission: the primary diagnosis, the comorbidity load, the length of stay, the volume of in-hospital procedures, and the patient’s prior healthcare utilisation. These are the features I expect to drive readmission risk, and §5 will quantify exactly how strongly each one does. What I’m doing here is the structural step before the signal step: showing the shape of each feature, so that the per-feature readmission rates that appear later are read against the right population baseline.
The section closes with a Mann-Whitney U battery — a single statistical pass that compares the distribution of every continuous clinical feature between readmitted and not-readmitted patients, and ranks them by rank-biserial effect size. This is the first formal signal-ranking exercise in the notebook, and the ranking it produces sets up the rest of the analysis: the top-of-list features get full distributional overlays in §6.2, and the strongest predictors carry directly into the modelling decisions in §7’s univariate league table.

3.1 Primary diagnosis groups
The raw diag_1 column holds the patient’s primary ICD-9 diagnosis code at admission, with 716 distinct values in the modelling cohort. Working with that level of granularity is impractical: most codes appear in fewer than 50 admissions, the long tail dilutes any signal, and one-hot encoding would produce a dimensionality the model cannot use. The Silver layer’s diag_1_group collapses these 716 codes into nine clinical groups plus a residual “Other” bucket, using the standard ICD-9 grouping convention from Strack et al. (2014): Circulatory, Respiratory, Digestive, Diabetes, Injury, Musculoskeletal, Genitourinary, Neoplasms, Other. A tiny Missing category (20 admissions) catches rows where the underlying ICD-9 code didn’t map to any group.


📊 Category Summary

column: diag_1_group | total_n: 99,340 | n_unique: 10 | displayed: 10 | hidden: 0 | displayed_share_%: 100.00

category: Circulatory | count: 29680 | pct_of_total: 29.88 | 

category: Other | count: 17793 | pct_of_total: 17.91 | 

category: Respiratory | count: 13934 | pct_of_total: 14.03 | 

category: Digestive | count: 9333 | pct_of_total: 9.40 | 

category: Diabetes | count: 8661 | pct_of_total: 8.72 | 

category: Injury | count: 6851 | pct_of_total: 6.90 | 

category: Genitourinary | count: 5002 | pct_of_total: 5.04 | 

category: Musculoskeletal | count: 4935 | pct_of_total: 4.97 | 

category: Neoplasms | count: 3131 | pct_of_total: 3.15 | 

category: Missing | count: 20 | pct_of_total: 0.02 |
The distribution shows the expected dominance of cardiovascular admissions in a diabetic cohort. Circulatory diagnoses lead at 29.88% of admissions (29,680), unsurprising given that cardiovascular comorbidity is the rule rather than the exception in diabetic inpatients. The “Other” bucket — the residual category for 716-code long tail entries that don’t map to one of the nine clinical groups — is the second-largest at 17.91% (17,793). Respiratory sits at 14.03% (13,934), Digestive at 9.40% (9,333), and Diabetes itself as the primary diagnosis at 8.72% (8,661) — meaning that in roughly nine out of ten admissions in this cohort, diabetes is comorbid rather than primary. Injury at 6.90%, Genitourinary at 5.04%, Musculoskeletal at 4.97%, and Neoplasms at 3.15% round out the distribution. The tiny Missing category holds just 20 admissions (0.02%).
Two analytical implications fall out. First, the diabetes-as-primary subgroup is small but interpretable: when a patient is admitted specifically for a diabetic event (DKA, hypoglycaemic crisis, severe hyperglycaemia), §5.3 will check whether they readmit at a different rate than patients admitted for cardiovascular or respiratory reasons with diabetes as a background condition. Second, the engineered n_comorbidity_flags feature in the next subsection will quantify how many of the three diagnosis positions carry a clinically grouped diagnosis — which is the difference between a single-system admission (one circulatory flag) and a multi-system one (circulatory + respiratory + diabetes simultaneously). The modelling notebook will lean heavily on the comorbidity flag count and on the per-group readmission rates that §5.3 produces.


3.2 Comorbidity load
The engineered n_comorbidity_flags feature counts how many of the three diagnosis positions on the admission record (diag_1, diag_2, diag_3) carry a code that maps to one of the three target clinical groups: circulatory, respiratory, or diabetes. The count ranges from 0 (none of the three positions carry one of those groups) to 3 (all three positions do). The intuition is that multi-system involvement is a stronger predictor of readmission than any single primary diagnosis — a patient simultaneously presenting cardiovascular, respiratory, and diabetic conditions is a fundamentally different risk profile from one with a single isolated condition.


📊 Category Summary

column: n_comorbidity_flags | total_n: 99,340 | n_unique: 4 | displayed: 4 | hidden: 0 | displayed_share_%: 100.00

category: 2 | count: 50517 | pct_of_total: 50.85 | 

category: 1 | count: 32662 | pct_of_total: 32.88 | 

category: 3 | count: 13950 | pct_of_total: 14.04 | 

category: 0 | count: 2211 | pct_of_total: 2.23 |
The modal value is 2 — most diabetic admissions present with two of the three target comorbidity classes coded across their diagnosis positions. The exact distribution: flag count 2 dominates at 50.85% of the cohort (50,517 admissions), flag count 1 at 32.88% (32,662), flag count 3 at 14.04% (13,950), and flag count 0 at just 2.23% (2,211). The mass is concentrated heavily in counts 1 and 2, which together hold 83.7% of admissions.
Two analytical points follow. First, the modal-2 result confirms the engineered feature is well-calibrated for this cohort — the median admission carries two of the three target comorbidity flags, which is exactly the multi-system pattern the count was designed to capture. The Mann-Whitney U battery in §3.7 will tell me whether the difference between flag counts of 1, 2, and 3 actually translates to different readmission rates, and §6.1’s quantile-binned plot will visualise that relationship directly.
Second, the flag count 0 subgroup is small but worth a thought. These admissions are diabetic — by construction; this is a diabetic-patient cohort — but their primary clinical issue at this admission was something other than circulatory, respiratory, or diabetic. They might be readmitted at a different rate than the multi-system admissions, and if they are, the modelling notebook needs to make sure the n_comorbidity_flags = 0 category is not lost in encoding. §7’s univariate league table will surface that question implicitly through the diag_1_is_* dummy rankings.


3.3 Length of stay distribution


📊 Distribution Summary
column: time_in_hospital | count: 99340 | mean: 4.38 | median: 4.00 | std: 2.97 | min: 1.00 | p5: 1.00 | p95: 11.00 | p99: 14.00 | max: 14.00 | skew: 1.14 | kurtosis: 0.89 |


📊 Boxplot Summary Statistics
column: time_in_hospital | count: 99340 | min: 1.00 | q1: 2.00 | median: 4.00 | q3: 6.00 | max: 14.00 | range: 13.00 | iqr: 4.00 | skew: 1.14 | kurtosis: 0.89 | number_of_outliers: 2147 | outliers_zscore: 995 |
The two plots together give the full picture: a histogram with the printed Distribution Summary, and a boxplot with the printed Boxplot Summary Statistics. Length of stay is right-skewed with a mean of 4.38 days, a median of 4 days, and a standard deviation of 2.97 days. The Q1–Q3 range is 2 to 6 days, and the maximum is censored at 14 days. The 95th percentile is 11 days and the 99th percentile 14 days — the right tail compresses against the censoring cap. The skew is 1.14 with a kurtosis of 0.89 — heavier in the right tail than a normal distribution but not dramatically so.
The IQR-based outlier count is 2,147 admissions, with 995 of them flagged as 3-sigma outliers on the z-score test. In a clinical context these are not data-quality outliers — they are clinically meaningful long stays, with the modal long-stay admission sitting at the 14-day censoring cap. The right tail represents patients with severe complications, multiple procedures, or post-acute recovery needs that prevented earlier discharge; their readmission risk is substantively higher than the median patient’s, and §5.5 will quantify that directly.
Two analytical threads pick up later. First, length of stay enters the modelling notebook as a continuous feature, and the right-skew is mild enough that no log transform is necessary — the modelling pipeline will use the raw integer values. Second, length of stay shows up in §9 as a confounder for the HbA1c testing question: longer-stay patients have more time and opportunity for the lab order, and the propensity-score model in §8.4 will need to control for it.


3.4 Lab procedure volume


📊 Distribution Summary
column: num_lab_procedures | count: 99340 | mean: 42.91 | median: 44.00 | std: 19.61 | min: 1.00 | p5: 4.00 | p95: 73.00 | p99: 84.00 | max: 132.00 | skew: -0.24 | kurtosis: -0.25 |
The Distribution Summary anchors the shape: mean 42.91, median 44.00, std 19.61, min 1.00, p5 4.00, p95 73.00, p99 84.00, max 132.00, with skew −0.24 and kurtosis −0.25. The negative skew is small but real. Visually, while the absolute maximum (132) stretches out a long right tail, the skewness is driven negative because the median sits above the mean, heavily weighted by a dense concentration of admissions between 40 and 60 procedures alongside a sharp, distinct spike of low-intensity admissions right at the left boundary. The kurtosis just below 0 means it has slightly thinner tails than a normal distribution, tapering off predictably past the 95th percentile.
Mechanically, this feature counts the total number of laboratory procedures ordered during the admission. It is essentially a proxy for clinical attention intensity: a sicker or more diagnostically uncertain patient generates more lab orders, and a routine admission generates fewer. Reading the feature this way matters when interpreting any predictive signal it carries — num_lab_procedures is unlikely to be a cause of readmission risk, but it is likely to be a correlate of underlying clinical complexity, which is itself the cause. The modelling notebook will use the raw count as a continuous feature; the SHAP analysis in notebook 02 will show whether the feature contributes meaningfully and whether it does so in the direction the proxy interpretation predicts.


3.5 Prior utilisation
The engineered n_prior_visits_total feature aggregates the patient’s outpatient, emergency, and inpatient visit counts in the year preceding the index admission. It is one of the strongest candidate predictors I expect to find: high prior utilisation indicates a patient who is already in active contact with the healthcare system, with chronic conditions or unstable management driving repeated visits, and that pattern almost mechanically extends into post-discharge readmission risk.
The chart below uses a log-scaled x-axis. The log scale is essential here — the raw distribution is dominated by patients with zero prior visits, and a linear-scale histogram would compress the tail into invisibility.


📊 Distribution Summary
column: n_prior_visits_total | count: 99340 | mean: 1.20 | median: 0.00 | std: 2.29 | min: 0.00 | p5: 0.00 | p95: 5.00 | p99: 10.00 | max: 80.00 | skew: 5.35 | kurtosis: 68.06 |
The Distribution Summary anchors the shape: mean 1.20, median 0, std 2.29, with a maximum of 80 prior visits, skew 5.35 and kurtosis 68.06 — the distribution is dramatically heavy-tailed. Most admissions come from patients with zero or low prior visits: the 5th and 50th percentiles are both 0, the 95th percentile is 5, and the 99th percentile is 10. The very long tail past 10 visits represents a small group of very high-utilisation patients, and the maximum value of 80 is the single most extreme admission in the cohort.
The bimodal-by-construction shape — a large mass at zero plus a long thin tail — has direct modelling implications. Linear models will struggle with this distribution unless it is transformed, because the zero-mass dominates any linear coefficient and pulls the fitted relationship toward zero. Tree models handle it natively because they split on raw thresholds. §6.2 below shows the distribution overlaid by readmission status, which is where this feature really earns its place: the readmitted patients are visibly shifted into the long tail relative to the not-readmitted patients, and the rank-biserial correlation in §3.7 will quantify that shift formally.
The high-utilisation tail is also the subgroup most likely to drive any aggregate effect. A small fraction of patients with disproportionately high prior visit counts can dominate group-level statistics, and §6.1’s quantile-binned readmission rate will show whether the readmission rate climbs monotonically with prior visits or whether it plateaus at the very top.


3.6 Length of stay by primary diagnosis


📊 Boxplot Summary Statistics (per category)

category: Digestive | count: 9333 | min: 1.00 | q1: 2.00 | median: 4.00 | q3: 6.00 | max: 14.00 | range: 13.00 | iqr: 4.00 | skew: 1.16 | kurtosis: 1.05 | number_of_outliers: 152 | outliers_zscore: 152 | 

category: Genitourinary | count: 5002 | min: 1.00 | q1: 2.00 | median: 3.00 | q3: 6.00 | max: 14.00 | range: 13.00 | iqr: 4.00 | skew: 1.19 | kurtosis: 1.10 | number_of_outliers: 72 | outliers_zscore: 72 |
