category: Musculoskeletal | count: 4935 | min: 1.00 | q1: 3.00 | median: 3.00 | q3: 5.00 | max: 14.00 | range: 13.00 | iqr: 2.00 | skew: 1.48 | kurtosis: 2.76 | number_of_outliers: 271 | outliers_zscore: 74 | 

category: Neoplasms | count: 3131 | min: 1.00 | q1: 3.00 | median: 5.00 | q3: 7.00 | max: 14.00 | range: 13.00 | iqr: 4.00 | skew: 0.74 | kurtosis: -0.24 | number_of_outliers: 52 | outliers_zscore: 0 | 

category: Other | count: 17793 | min: 1.00 | q1: 2.00 | median: 4.00 | q3: 6.00 | max: 14.00 | range: 13.00 | iqr: 4.00 | skew: 1.07 | kurtosis: 0.49 | number_of_outliers: 640 | outliers_zscore: 0 | 

category: Respiratory | count: 13934 | min: 1.00 | q1: 2.00 | median: 3.00 | q3: 6.00 | max: 14.00 | range: 13.00 | iqr: 4.00 | skew: 1.16 | kurtosis: 0.94 | number_of_outliers: 231 | outliers_zscore: 231 |
The boxplot stratifies length of stay across the nine diagnosis groups, with summary statistics printed for each. The medians and IQRs are surprisingly similar: most diagnosis groups have a median LOS of 3–4 days and a Q3 of 5–7 days. The boxes overlap heavily — most diabetic admissions take roughly the same time to clear regardless of the triggering diagnosis.
A few groups stand out modestly. Neoplasms has the highest median at 5 days and the widest Q3 at 7 days — cancer-related admissions tend to be more complex and take longer to discharge (n=3,131; skew 0.74, the most symmetric of any group). Circulatory, the largest group by far (n=29,680), sits at a median of 3 days and dominates the cohort’s overall LOS distribution. Injury has a higher Q1 at 3 days than most groups, suggesting that even the shortest injury admissions take longer to clear than the shortest admissions of other types — likely reflecting required observation periods after trauma. Musculoskeletal is unusually compact (IQR = 2 days, kurtosis 2.76) — the tightest stay-length distribution in the cohort.
The “Missing” category is a tiny stratum (20 admissions) and its boxplot is not informative — the small sample is noted for transparency but does not enter any analytical claim.
The modest variation across diagnosis groups is itself useful information for the modelling notebook. It tells me that length of stay is not heavily confounded with primary diagnosis — the two features carry largely independent information, which means notebook 02 can use them both as covariates without worrying that one is a noisy proxy for the other.


3.7 Mann-Whitney U battery — continuous clinical features vs readmission
This is the first formal statistical battery in the notebook. For each continuous clinical feature, I run a Mann-Whitney U test comparing the feature’s distribution between readmitted (readmitted_30d == 1) and not-readmitted (readmitted_30d == 0) patients, then report the rank-biserial correlation — a unit-free effect size between -1 and +1 that quantifies the magnitude of the distributional shift.
I use Mann-Whitney rather than a t-test for two reasons. First, several of the continuous features (prior visits, number of inpatient visits, number of emergency visits) are heavily right-skewed with mass concentrated at zero — exactly the conditions under which the t-test’s normality assumption breaks. Second, the rank-biserial r is more robust to outliers than Pearson’s r, and the cohort has plenty of clinically-meaningful long-tail outliers in features like n_prior_visits_total that would distort a parametric comparison.
The output below ranks every continuous clinical feature by absolute rank-biserial r, descending. This ranking sets up the rest of the notebook: the top features get full distributional overlays in §6.2, the strongest predictors carry into §7’s univariate league table, and the modelling notebook in 02 will spend most of its feature-importance attention on the top of this list.
Mann-Whitney U battery — continuous clinical features vs readmitted_30d
===============================================================================================

5        num_medications         16.0000            15.0000 541,381,148.0000   0.0000          -0.0872 0.0872
6       number_emergency          0.0000             0.0000 529,815,600.5000   0.0000          -0.0640 0.0640

8         n_meds_changed          0.0000             0.0000 524,189,520.5000   0.0000          -0.0527 0.0527
9     num_lab_procedures         45.0000            44.0000 519,788,577.0000   0.0000          -0.0438 0.0438

11     number_outpatient          0.0000             0.0000 518,223,877.0000   0.0000          -0.0407 0.0407

The ranking is decisive and clinically interpretable. Prior utilisation features dominate the top of the list. number_inpatient (prior inpatient visits in the preceding year) carries a rank-biserial r = −0.214, the largest absolute effect size in the table. n_prior_visits_total follows at r = −0.208, The drop to third place is sharp: time_in_hospital sits at r = -0.095, with number_diagnoses (r = -0.88) and num_medications (r = −0.087) close behind. The negative sign means the readmitted patients have higher values on these features (the rank-biserial is computed so that a negative r indicates the readmitted group is shifted upward in the rank ordering).
Below the top five, the effect sizes drop further. number_emergency at r = −0.064, med_change_ratio at r = −0.059, n_meds_changed at r = −0.053, num_lab_procedures at r = −0.044, age_midpoint at *r = −0.043, number_outpatient at **r = −0.041 — all in the negligible band by Cohen’s bands. The bottom of the table holds features with rank-biserial r values close to zero: num_procedures (r = +0.008, p = 0.15, not significant), n_comorbidity_flags (r = −0.007, p = 0.18, not significant), n_meds_prescribed (r = −0.007, p = 0.20, not significant).. The non-significance of these three is noteworthy — they are the only continuous features in the battery whose Mann-Whitney p-values do not reject independence with the target.
A note on Cohen’s interpretation bands for rank-biserial r. Conventionally, |r| < 0.10 is negligible, 0.10 ≤ |r| < 0.30 is small, 0.30 ≤ |r| < 0.50 is moderate, and |r| ≥ 0.50 is large. By that standard, only number_inpatient and n_prior_visits_total cross from negligible into small territory — no single continuous feature in this cohort reaches a moderate effect size on the readmission target on its own. This is consistent with the published literature on this dataset, which reports AUC ceilings in the 0.65–0.70 band for readmission prediction; the signal is genuinely diffuse, and the modelling notebook’s job will be to combine many small effects into a useful aggregate score rather than to ride a single dominant predictor.
The full ranking points forward to two specific sections. §6.1 takes the top-six features by effect size and renders the rate-by-quantile plot for each, which surfaces the shape of the relationship. §7’s univariate league table extends the same exercise to categorical features.

title: Health Analytics & Biostatistics — Exploratory Analysis of a Diabetic Inpatient Cohort
text:
4 · The Medication Picture
This dataset has 23 medication columns covering individual diabetic agents and combination therapies — metformin, glipizide, glyburide, insulin, and 19 others, each recorded as one of {No, Steady, Up, Down} indicating whether the medication was prescribed and how its dose changed during the admission. Most of these columns are sparse: the diagnostic in §1 already flagged 13 medication columns as near-zero-variance and 2 columns (examide, citoglipton) as fully constant.
This section profiles the medication landscape in three steps. First, the high-level binary diabetes_med flag and the dominant insulin regimen breakdown — the two columns that carry meaningful variance. Second, a panel grid showing the near-zero-variance landscape so the reader can see exactly how thin the long tail is. Third, the change flag and its association with the readmission target. The point is to motivate the drop-list decisions the modelling notebook will make: which medications stay as features, which get aggregated into engineered counts, which are dropped entirely.

4.1 Diabetes medication prescribed
The diabetes_med column is a high-level binary flag indicating whether any diabetic medication was prescribed during the admission. It collapses the 23 individual medication columns into a single yes/no indicator that the modelling notebook can use without engaging the full sparse medication landscape.


📊 Category Summary

column: diabetes_med | total_n: 99,340 | n_unique: 2 | displayed: 2 | hidden: 0 | displayed_share_%: 100.00

category: Yes | count: 76717 | pct_of_total: 77.23 | 

category: No | count: 22623 | pct_of_total: 22.77 |
Yes 77.23% (76,717 admissions), No 22.77% (22,623). Roughly three-quarters of admissions have at least one diabetic medication on the chart, leaving a substantial 22.77% without. In a diabetic-patient cohort that is itself an interesting subgroup. The 22.77% no-medication admissions are most likely either patients managed by lifestyle intervention alone (Type 2 diabetes in early stages or well-controlled), patients admitted for non-diabetic reasons where the home medication regimen was held during the admission, or patients whose diabetes is documented in the diagnosis codes but whose inpatient medication chart simply does not record diabetic agents.
The split is meaningful for the modelling notebook in two ways. First, the binary flag is itself a usable feature — §7’s univariate league table will quantify how strongly it associates with the readmission target. Second, the 22.77% no-medication subgroup will need to be cleanly distinguishable from the 77.23% medicated subgroup in any feature engineering that involves the medication columns; the engineered n_meds_prescribed count handles this by summing across the 23 columns, with the no-medication subgroup landing at zero.


4.2 Insulin regimen breakdown
Insulin is the most frequently used medication in this cohort and is the single drug column with enough variance to carry useful signal on its own. Unlike the other 22 medication columns, insulin has all four status levels populated meaningfully: No (no insulin during admission), Steady (continued at home dose), Up (dose increased), Down (dose decreased).


📊 Category Summary

column: insulin | total_n: 99,340 | n_unique: 4 | displayed: 4 | hidden: 0 | displayed_share_%: 100.00

category: No | count: 46376 | pct_of_total: 46.68 | 

category: Steady | count: 30069 | pct_of_total: 30.27 | 

category: Down | count: 11908 | pct_of_total: 11.99 | 

category: Up | count: 10987 | pct_of_total: 11.06 |
The breakdown: No 46.68% (46,376), Steady 30.27% (30,069), Down 11.99% (11,908), Up 11.06% (10,987). About 53% of admissions have insulin on the regimen, with Steady being the dominant active status — the patient continued whatever home regimen they were on. The Up and Down categories together account for 23.05% of admissions, meaning a non-trivial fraction of patients had their insulin dose actively adjusted during the stay (slightly more Down-titrations than Up-titrations).
The dose-adjustment categories are clinically informative. An Up titration during admission signals that the inpatient team identified inadequate glycaemic control on the home regimen and intensified treatment; a Down titration signals the opposite. Both are clinical decisions that reflect the team’s read of the patient’s diabetic status, and both could plausibly correlate with readmission risk in opposite directions — §7’s league table will surface whether they do.
The four-level structure makes insulin one of the few medication columns that survives notebook 02’s drop list intact. Most of the other 22 medication columns will be either dropped (the two fully constant ones) or aggregated into engineered counts (the 13 near-zero-variance ones). Insulin enters the model as its own categorical feature, and §7’s league table will rank it alongside the engineered features to confirm the decision was right.


4.3 Near-zero-variance medication landscape
The diagnostic in §1 flagged 13 medication columns as near-zero-variance and 2 columns (examide, citoglipton) as fully constant — every row in the cohort has the same value. The flag is a warning that the column carries essentially no usable variance for the modelling notebook: a feature where 99%+ of rows share a single value cannot reliably distinguish between readmitted and not-readmitted patients on its own.
The chart below renders all 16 flagged columns as a 4×4 panel grid, with each panel showing the count distribution of one column. The point of the visualisation is to make the sparsity vivid — not to extract analytical signal, but to show the reader what “near-zero-variance” actually looks like at this scale.

Each of the sixteen panels tells the same story: a single value (almost always No) covers more than 99% of the column, with the remaining values appearing as tiny slivers at the bottom of the bar. The visual confirms what the diagnostic flagged numerically — these columns carry effectively zero usable variance.
For the modelling notebook this confirms my plan. The two fully constant columns (examide, citoglipton) get dropped unconditionally — they cannot improve any model under any encoding. The 13 near-zero-variance columns get either dropped or aggregated into the engineered n_meds_prescribed and n_meds_changed counts that already capture whatever residual information they hold. Including them as standalone features would inflate the model’s dimensionality without adding signal, and a regularised linear model would zero them out anyway.
The next subsection prints the inventory in tabular form for narrative reference, with the dominant-value share and the count of non-dominant rows per column.


4.4 NZV companion summary table
For narrative reference, here is the near-zero-variance inventory in tabular form: the dominant value, its share of the column, the number of unique values, and the count of non-dominant rows for each of the 16 flagged medication columns.

The table makes the asymmetry explicit. The two fully constant columns — examide and citoglipton — sit at 100% dominance with 0 minority rows and a single unique value each; they will be dropped unconditionally. Below them, several columns have fewer than 100 minority rows out of 99,340 admissions: acetohexamide (1), glimepiride_pioglitazone (1), metformin_pioglitazone (1), metformin_rosiglitazone (2), troglitazone (3), glipizide_metformin (13), tolbutamide (21), miglitol (38), tolazamide (39), chlorpropamide (85) — far too sparse to support stable coefficient estimates in any linear model and providing essentially no split power for tree models either.
The bottom of the table holds the columns with marginally more variance: acarbose at 305 minority rows, nateglinide at 689, and glyburide_metformin at 698 non-dominant rows. These three are still near-zero-variance by the conventional >99% dominance threshold, but they carry enough non-dominant rows that an aggressive modelling experiment might keep them as engineered indicator flags. The pragmatic choice for notebook 02 is to drop all 13 near-zero-variance columns and let the engineered medication aggregates (n_meds_prescribed, n_meds_changed, med_change_ratio) carry whatever signal they collectively hold.


4.5 Medication regimen change
The change column flags whether any diabetic medication was added, removed, or had its dose changed during the admission, taking values Ch (changed) or No (no change). This is potentially informative — clinical decisions to adjust a regimen mid-admission reflect the inpatient team’s judgement about how well the patient was being managed before, and that judgement may correlate with the readmission risk going forward.


📊 Category Summary

column: change | total_n: 99,340 | n_unique: 2 | displayed: 2 | hidden: 0 | displayed_share_%: 100.00

category: No | count: 53220 | pct_of_total: 53.57 |

Chi-square test of independence: change × readmitted_30d
============================================================

  H₁ : medication regimen change and readmitted_30d are associated

  Effect size — Cohen's conventions for Cramér's V (dof = 1)

Readmission rate by regimen change status (%):
change
Ch    12.02

The split is No 53.57% (53,220) / Ch 46.43% (46,120) — close to balanced. The chi-square test is statistically significant (χ² = 34.15 on 1 degree of freedom, p ≈ 0), but the effect size is Cramér’s V = 0.0183 — negligible by Cohen’s conventions. This is, again, the large-N paradox: with 99,340 admissions, a tiny departure from independence becomes statistically detectable, and the p-value alone is uninformative about whether the association matters analytically.
The per-status readmission rates make the size of the effect concrete: the Ch (changed) arm readmits at 12.02%, and the No (unchanged) arm readmits at 10.84% — a 1.18 percentage point absolute difference. The direction is the one I would expect: patients whose regimen was actively adjusted during the stay readmit at a slightly higher rate, consistent with the interpretation that a regimen change is a marker of an underlying clinical instability rather than a prophylactic adjustment. But the magnitude is too small to drive predictive modelling on its own, and the modelling notebook will use the change_flag column primarily as a small-effect input that the gradient-boosting models can combine with stronger features.
A note for the modelling pipeline. The change column is a string-form duplicate of the engineered change_flag integer column the Silver layer produces; both encode the same underlying signal. Notebook 02’s preprocessing will drop change and keep change_flag to avoid feeding the same information twice into the model. §7’s univariate league table makes that redundancy visible (both appear at the same Cramér’s V).

title: Health Analytics & Biostatistics — Exploratory Analysis of a Diabetic Inpatient Cohort
text:
5 · The Target — 30-Day Readmission
This section profiles the target variable in isolation, then stratifies it across age bands, primary diagnosis, discharge disposition, and length-of-stay quantiles. The point of the section is to give a clear baseline rate for the cohort, then to show which features carry the most signal visually and statistically before the formal bivariate scan in §6 and §7 produces the consolidated ranking.
A note on the test choice. For each stratifying variable I pair the readmission-rate visualisation with an appropriate hypothesis test: chi-square for categorical strata, Kruskal-Wallis for ordered categorical strata where the rank-based test is more appropriate than the nominal one. Each test reports both a p-value and an effect size (Cramér’s V or epsilon-squared), and I read both together — the p-value tells me whether the effect is detectable, the effect size tells me whether it matters.

5.1 Class balance


📊 Category Summary

column: readmitted_30d | total_n: 99,340 | n_unique: 2 | displayed: 2 | hidden: 0 | displayed_share_%: 100.00

category: 0 | count: 88026 | pct_of_total: 88.61 | 

category: 1 | count: 11314 | pct_of_total: 11.39 | 

Positive class rate: 11.39%
Imbalance ratio (negative:positive): 7.8 : 1
The positive class rate is 11.39% (11,314 admissions readmitted within 30 days, 88,026 not) — moderately imbalanced but not extreme. The imbalance ratio is 7.8 to 1 (negative to positive), meaning a baseline classifier predicting “no readmission” for everyone would achieve 88.61% accuracy while having zero clinical utility. This is the canonical class-imbalance situation, and accuracy is the wrong evaluation metric for it; notebook 02 will lean on ROC-AUC and PR-AUC as the primary ranking metrics and on Youden’s J for threshold optimisation.
The 11.39% rate also calibrates expectations for the modelling chapter. The published literature on this dataset reports AUC ceilings in the 0.65–0.70 band — meaning even strong models on this cohort produce only modest discriminative power, and the goal is a defensible, well-diagnosed model rather than a Kaggle-style chase of the last decimal point. Class-weighted training and SMOTE oversampling are both planned as part of the imbalance ladder in notebook 02, and the threshold-optimisation step will surface the recall/precision trade-off explicitly so the operating point can be chosen by the clinical team rather than baked in by default.
A second implication: the imbalance is mild enough that the 11.39% positive class will appear in every cross-validation fold with reasonable density. §11 confirms that the patient-level GroupKFold split produces five folds with nearly identical positive rates, which means any cross-fold variance in modelling metrics will reflect genuine model variability rather than fold-level imbalance.


5.2 Readmission rate by age band


📊 Target Rate Summary (per category) — overall = 11.39%

category: [0-10) | n: 160 | rate_%: 1.88 | ci_low_%: 0.64 | ci_high_%: 5.37 | 

category: [10-20) | n: 690 | rate_%: 5.80 | ci_low_%: 4.29 | ci_high_%: 7.80 | 

category: [20-30) | n: 1649 | rate_%: 14.31 | ci_low_%: 12.70 | ci_high_%: 16.08 | 

category: [30-40) | n: 3764 | rate_%: 11.26 | ci_low_%: 10.29 | ci_high_%: 12.31 | 

category: [40-50) | n: 9607 | rate_%: 10.66 | ci_low_%: 10.06 | ci_high_%: 11.29 | 

category: [50-60) | n: 17060 | rate_%: 9.77 | ci_low_%: 9.33 | ci_high_%: 10.23 | 

category: [60-70) | n: 22058 | rate_%: 11.30 | ci_low_%: 10.89 | ci_high_%: 11.73 | 

category: [70-80) | n: 25329 | rate_%: 12.06 | ci_low_%: 11.66 | ci_high_%: 12.46 | 

category: [80-90) | n: 16434 | rate_%: 12.57 | ci_low_%: 12.07 | ci_high_%: 13.08 | 

category: [90-100) | n: 2589 | rate_%: 11.90 | ci_low_%: 10.71 | ci_high_%: 13.20 |
The chart and the printed table together tell two stories.
The expected story: readmission rate climbs steadily across the senior bands, from [60-70) at 11.30% through [70-80) at 12.06% to a peak in [80-90) at 12.57%, then easing slightly in [90-100) at 11.90%. The youngest paediatric bands sit far below the cohort average — [0-10) at 1.88% and [10-20) at 5.80% — though both are sample-size-thin (160 and 690 admissions respectively, with Wilson 95% CIs of [0.64%, 5.37%] and [4.29%, 7.80%]) and per-band claims about them carry wide uncertainty. The working-age bands [40-50) at 10.66% and [50-60) at 9.77% sit just below the cohort average of 11.39%.
The unexpected story: the [20-30) band readmits at 14.31% — the highest single rate in the cohort, even above the [80-90) peak. The 95% Wilson CI is [12.70%, 16.08%], and it does not overlap the working-age bands’ CIs (the [50-60) CI tops out at 10.23%, the [60-70) CI tops out at 11.73%), so the spike is statistically distinguishable, not just sample noise. The clinical reading is familiar in the diabetic-readmission literature: young adults aged 20–30 with diabetes tend to be Type 1 patients with poorly controlled glycaemic management, often presenting in DKA or hypoglycaemic crisis, with social and adherence factors driving repeat admissions. Their readmission dynamics are fundamentally different from older adults with Type 2 diabetes, even though the absolute rates land in similar territory.
The bracket-level pattern matters for two analytical decisions. First, my engineered age_midpoint_squared feature is well-justified — a strictly linear age term would underfit both the bend in the youngest bands and the [20-30) spike. The quadratic gives the linear models some curvature to work with, though even the quadratic won’t capture the [20-30) spike cleanly; that’s a non-monotone pattern that benefits from tree models or an interaction with diabetes type (which I don’t have in this cohort). Second, the within-senior-band differentiation will be where the modelling notebook earns most of its age signal: the contrast between [60-70), [70-80), and [80-90) is small (1.27 pp between min and max) but consistent, and those three bands together hold 64.0% of the cohort, so even a small per-band rate differential translates to substantial population-level signal.
Kruskal-Wallis test: readmitted_30d across age bands
============================================================
  H₀ : the distribution of readmitted_30d is identical across age bands
  H₁ : at least one age band differs in its readmitted_30d distribution
  α  : 0.05
------------------------------------------------------------
  H statistic        =      133.623
  Degrees of freedom = 9
  p-value            = 0.0000
  k groups           = 10
  Total n            = 99,340
  Epsilon-squared ε² = 0.0013

  Effect size — Cohen's conventions for ε² (Kruskal-Wallis analogue of η²)
     negligible: ε² < 0.01  |  small: 0.01–0.06  |  moderate: 0.06–0.14  |  large: ε² ≥ 0.14
     → observed ε² = 0.0013 → negligible
------------------------------------------------------------
  Decision : REJECT H₀ at α = 0.05  (p = 0.0000 < 0.05)
  Reading  : At least one age band differs in its readmission distribution,
             with a negligible effect size. The test does not say which
             band(s) drive the difference — read the rate-by-band visual
             alongside this for that interpretation.
The Kruskal-Wallis test asks whether the readmission distribution is identical across all 10 age bands. With H = 133.62 on 9 degrees of freedom and p ≈ 0, the null hypothesis of identical distributions is rejected decisively. The effect size, measured as epsilon-squared, is ε² = 0.0013 — negligible by Cohen’s conventions for ε² (small ≥ 0.01, moderate ≥ 0.06, large ≥ 0.14).
This is, again, the large-N paradox: the test is detecting a real but tiny effect. Age band is a real signal — the visual makes that evident, especially the [20-30) spike — but the overall spread of rates around the 11.39% mean accounts for only a fraction of a percent of the variance in readmission risk. The test does not tell me which band(s) drive the difference, which is why I read the rate-by-band table above alongside it. The modelling notebook will use age primarily through interactions (the engineered prior_visits_x_age term in particular) rather than as a standalone main effect, and the SHAP analysis in notebook 02 will quantify that decomposition directly.

The spread between best and worst is 3.56 percentage points — a real but modest differential, and one that will translate to a meaningful split in any tree model that branches on diag_1_group. Two readings stand out. First, the Diabetes-as-primary subgroup readmits at the highest rate even though it is small (8.72% of the cohort) — a clinically intuitive finding. When a patient is admitted specifically for a diabetic event (DKA, hypoglycaemic crisis, severe hyperglycaemia), they are sicker on the underlying disease axis than a patient admitted for a cardiovascular event with diabetes as a background condition. Second, the Circulatory group — by far the largest at 29,680 admissions (29.88% of the cohort) — sits very close to the cohort mean of 11.39%, meaning circulatory admissions are essentially typical readmission risk; the population-level readmission signal is dominated by them not because they are high-risk individually but because they are numerous.
Two analytical threads pick up later. First, the per-group rates here are the basis for the target encoding of diag_1_group, diag_2_group, and diag_3_group that the modelling notebook applies in its preprocessing step — each level gets converted to its per-level readmission rate, which compresses the categorical structure into a single numeric value while preserving the discriminative information the chart shows. ------------------------------------------------------------

  Effect size — Cohen's conventions for Cramér's V (dof = 1)

             by-disposition visual alongside this to see which dispositions

The chi-square test is significant (χ² = 1,322 on 20 degrees of freedom, p ≈ 0), and Cramér’s V = 0.115 — landing in the small band, the strongest categorical effect surfaced anywhere in the notebook. The printed per-disposition table makes the source of the effect concrete:

Discharged to home (60,232 admissions, the dominant disposition) readmits at 9.30% — well below the cohort average of 11.39%.
Discharged to home with home health service (12,902) readmits at 12.70%.
Discharged/transferred to SNF (13,954) readmits at 14.66% — meaningfully above average.
Discharged/transferred to another rehab fac (1,992) readmits at 27.71% — the highest sizeable disposition.
Discharged/transferred/referred to a psychiatric hospital (139) readmits at 36.69%, and a few small dispositions hit even higher rates but with sample sizes too small to support standalone claims.

The reading is clinically intuitive. A discharge to a skilled nursing facility (SNF) signals that the patient was not stable enough for independent living at the point of release, and SNF admissions are themselves a common pathway back to acute care. A home health services discharge signals a less acute but still elevated post-discharge care need. Both dispositions correlate with higher readmission risk because both are markers of the same underlying clinical instability that drives the readmission itself.
For the modelling notebook this is one of the strongest single-feature signals available. discharge_disposition_id will enter the model as a categorical feature, and §7’s univariate league table will confirm it sits near the top of the ranked list across all categorical features. The SHAP analysis in notebook 02 will quantify how much of the model’s predictive power flows through this feature specifically, and how much flows through the prior-utilisation features that §3.7 already flagged as the strongest continuous predictors.


5.5 Readmission rate by length of stay


📊 Target Rate Summary (per quantile) — overall = 11.39%

quantile: Q2 | bin_range: [2, 3] | n: 17432 | rate_%: 10.80 |

quantile: Q5 | bin_range: [5, 7] | n: 13051 | rate_%: 12.97 | 

quantile: Q6 | bin_range: [7, 9] | n: 7149 | rate_%: 14.46 | 

quantile: Q7 | bin_range: [9, 14] | n: 7562 | rate_%: 13.26 |
The chart bins length of stay into seven quantile groups (the qcut binning collapsed from 10 to 7 because LOS is integer-valued and many patients share the same exact stay length). The pattern is monotonic across the first six bins, then dips slightly at the top:

Q1 [1, 2 days] (n=30,713): 9.33% — the lowest
Q2 [2, 3] (n=17,432): 10.80%
Q3 [3, 4] (n=13,684): 11.99%
Q4 [4, 5] (n=9,749): 12.27%
Q5 [5, 7] (n=13,051): 12.97%
Q6 [7, 9] (n=7,149): 14.46% — the peak
Q7 [9, 14] (n=7,562): 13.26%

The longest-stay band readmits at 13.26%, which is 1.42× the shortest-stay band’s 9.33% — a meaningful gradient. The peak at Q6 [7–9 days] is interesting: very long stays may slightly underperform the 7–9-day band because they capture patients who were stabilised over the long admission and discharged to post-acute facilities (which themselves carry the strongest single-feature readmission signal in this cohort, per §5.4).
The reading is consistent with the §5.4 finding on discharge disposition. Long stays correlate with clinical complexity and with discharge to post-acute care (SNF, home health, transfer), and clinical complexity correlates with readmission risk. The relationship is unlikely to be causal in the simple direction the chart suggests — staying in the hospital one day longer does not cause readmission risk. Both the length of stay and the readmission risk are downstream effects of the same underlying clinical complexity.
For the modelling notebook this confirms time_in_hospital as a useful continuous predictor — it is monotone over its informative range, and §3.7’s Mann-Whitney battery already gave it a small but meaningful effect size. Tree models will branch on it cleanly; linear models will pick up most of the signal even with a linear coefficient.

title: Health Analytics & Biostatistics — Exploratory Analysis of a Diabetic Inpatient Cohort
text:
6 · Bivariate Signal Scan — Continuous Features
§3.7 already gave me a Mann-Whitney U ranking of every continuous clinical feature against the readmission target. This section extends that ranking with two complementary lenses: a rate-by-quantile plot for the top features (which surfaces the shape of the relationship — linear, monotonic, threshold), and a distributional overlay split by readmission status for the top two features (which shows where on the feature scale the readmitted patients concentrate). The section closes with a point-biserial correlation table that gives a single signed statistic per feature.
The point of the three lenses together is robustness. Mann-Whitney’s rank-biserial r tells me the magnitude of the distributional shift; the quantile-binned plot tells me the shape of the conditional readmission rate; the point-biserial r tells me the direction. If any of the three disagrees materially with the others, that’s a flag worth investigating; if they agree, the feature is a strong, interpretable candidate for the modelling notebook.

6.1 Quantile-binned readmission rate for top continuous features
I render the rate-by-quantile plot for the top six features by Mann-Whitney effect size from §3.7. The shape of each curve is informative: a monotonically increasing curve confirms a clean predictor, a U-shape suggests the relationship reverses at extreme values, and a flat curve indicates the feature is uninformative on a univariate basis even if a t-test or chi-square would call it significant.
The six features are: number_inpatient, n_prior_visits_total, number_emergency, time_in_hospital, n_comorbidity_flags, num_medications. Note that for integer-valued features with heavy zero-mass (the prior-utilisation triad in particular), pd.qcut collapses the requested 10 deciles down to fewer bins because of duplicate quantile boundaries — the printed summary blocks below show the exact binning each feature received.

The relationships are mostly monotone-increasing, with the strongest gradients in the prior-utilisation features. Reading from the printed per-quantile summaries:

number_inpatient — qcut collapsed to 3 bins because of the integer-zero-mass distribution. Bottom bin [0, 1] readmits at 9.63% (n=85,226); top bin [2, 21] readmits at 26.40% (n=6,814) — a 2.74× gradient, the steepest in the cohort. Patients with two or more prior inpatient admissions in the year before this one are the highest-risk subgroup the cohort surfaces.
n_prior_visits_total — 4 bins; bottom [0, 1] = 9.24%, top [3, 80] = 21.57% — a 2.33× gradient. Same shape as number_inpatient but with broader inclusion (outpatient and emergency visits add to the count).
number_emergency — only 2 bins because of integer-zero-mass. Bottom [0, 1] = 11.00% (essentially the cohort average), top [1, 76] = 21.71% — patients with any prior emergency visit are visibly elevated.
time_in_hospital — 7 bins, the monotone trend already surfaced in §5.5; top-vs-bottom 1.42×.
n_comorbidity_flags — 3 bins, essentially flat at 11.11% / 11.65% / 11.14%. The univariate signal is negligible, consistent with the cell 101 point-biserial correlation of 0.004 (p = 0.18, not significant). The flag count was built on the hypothesis that multi-system morbidity drives readmission risk, but on a univariate basis the cohort does not bear that out cleanly. The signal is likely there in interactions with other features (the modelling notebook’s SHAP analysis will surface it), but as a standalone main effect the comorbidity count is weaker than expected.
num_medications — 10 deciles; bottom [1, 7] = 8.27%, top [26, 81] = 12.98% — gentle upward slope, 1.57× ratio.

The shape of the number_inpatient curve in particular is worth pinning down. The steepest jump is between the [0, 1] bin and the [1, 2] bin (9.63% → 17.93%) — meaning even a single prior inpatient admission almost doubles the per-admission readmission rate. This is the kind of relationship a tree model will capture cleanly with a single split, and a regularised linear model will capture as a strong positive coefficient. The feature is going to drive a substantial fraction of the modelling notebook’s predictive power.


6.2 Distribution overlays for the top two features
For the top two features by effect size — number_inpatient and n_prior_visits_total — I show the full distributional overlay split by target. This lets me see where on the feature scale the readmitted patients concentrate relative to the not-readmitted patients. The rate-by-quantile plots above showed the conditional rate; these overlays show the underlying densities that the conditional rate is computed from.
The first plot uses linear scaling on the x-axis; the second uses log scaling because the n_prior_visits_total distribution has a heavy right tail that would otherwise compress into invisibility on a linear axis.


Both overlays show the same pattern: the readmitted distribution is shifted right relative to the not-readmitted distribution — readmitted patients are systematically the higher-utilisation patients. The two distributions overlap heavily on the left edge (most patients in both arms have zero or low prior visits), and the separation grows in the right tail (high-utilisation patients are over-represented in the readmitted arm).
The overlap region matters. Even though the readmitted distribution is shifted right, most of the cohort lies in the heavy overlap zone at the low end — meaning that for the typical patient, the prior-visit features alone do not separate the classes cleanly. The discriminative power comes from the tails: patients with very high prior-utilisation counts are reliably more likely to readmit, but most patients do not sit in those tails. A single feature cannot carry the prediction; the model needs to combine many small signals to score the bulk of the cohort, and the high-utilisation tail provides the strongest individual contribution.
This is exactly the substrate the published literature describes when it reports AUC ceilings of 0.65–0.70 for this dataset. There is no single feature that cleanly separates the classes, but there are many features that each contribute a small amount of discriminative information. Notebook 02’s gradient-boosted model will combine those contributions; the SHAP analysis will show how each feature contributes at the per-prediction level; and the calibration analysis will show whether the resulting probability scores are usable as risk estimates.


6.3 Point-biserial correlation table
The point-biserial correlation is the special case of Pearson’s r where one variable is binary. It gives a single signed statistic per continuous feature, which is useful for confirming both the magnitude (already established by the Mann-Whitney rank-biserial r) and the direction (positive r means the feature increases with the positive class; negative r means it decreases).
The output below ranks every continuous clinical feature by absolute point-biserial r, descending. The ranking should align broadly with the Mann-Whitney ranking from §3.7; meaningful disagreement between the two would flag a feature whose distributional shift is rank-based but not linear, or vice versa.

First, all signs are positive except num_procedures, which carries a tiny negative correlation of r = −0.011 (p = 0.0006, statistically significant only because of the large N). The negative direction is unexpected on a clinical reading — more procedures should correlate with sicker patients and therefore with higher readmission — but the magnitude is so small that the inverse direction is essentially noise. The modelling notebook will likely find that num_procedures enters with a weak positive coefficient through interactions with other features.
Second, three features have non-significant or near-zero correlations: n_comorbidity_flags at r = 0.004 (p = 0.18, not significant), n_meds_prescribed at r ≈ 0.001 (p = 0.77, not significant), and num_procedures at r = −0.011. The first two are particularly notable because they are engineered features built on plausible clinical hypotheses; their univariate weakness suggests the hypotheses they encode are either too coarse or only operate through interactions. The modelling notebook’s SHAP analysis will be the test of whether they earn their place.
With the continuous-feature scan complete, the next section runs the equivalent battery for categorical features, then consolidates both into a single univariate league table that ranks every feature in the cohort against the readmission target.

section: 7 · Bivariate Signal Scan — Categorical Features & Univariate Signal League Table
text:
7 · Bivariate Signal Scan — Categorical Features & Univariate Signal League Table
I now run a chi-square + Cramér’s V battery across every categorical feature in the cohort (excluding the target itself, the patient/encounter IDs, and the high-cardinality raw diagnosis codes that would not encode usefully in any modelling pipeline). The output is a single ranked table — the univariate league table — that gives the modelling notebook a feature-prioritisation input across both categorical and continuous types.
The chi-square test is appropriate for categorical features because it asks the right question: does the joint distribution of feature and target depart from independence? Cramér’s V converts the chi-square to a unit-free effect size between 0 and 1, with bias correction so that features of different cardinalities are comparable. By Cohen’s conventions (small ≥ 0.10, moderate ≥ 0.20, large ≥ 0.40), I expect very few features in this cohort to clear the small threshold — the published literature has already established that no single feature dominates readmission prediction on this dataset.

7.1 Visualising the league table
A ranked lollipop chart of the top 25 categorical features, sorted by Cramér’s V descending. The visual makes the league structure obvious — where the top is, where the negligible-effect cliff falls, and which feature families cluster together at each level.

The league table confirms the analytical structure I expected. medical_specialty sits at the top with Cramér’s V = 0.0550 — a negligible effect by Cohen’s bands but the strongest categorical association in this batch, almost certainly because the specialty mix proxies for underlying clinical complexity (cardiology, endocrinology, and emergency admissions readmit at different rates). insulin follows at V = 0.0444, and age at V = 0.0354, with the engineered diagnosis-group features (diag_3_group, diag_1_group, diag_2_group) filling out positions 4–6 around V = 0.025–0.035.
Below the top six, the effects fall into the negligible band uniformly. payer_code at V = 0.030, metformin at V = 0.026, diabetes_med and diabetes_med_flag (the same signal twice, once as a string and once as the engineered flag) tied at V = 0.0258, has_hba1c_tested at V = 0.020 (this is the treatment variable for notebook 03’s causal analysis — §8 will pick it up shortly), and the long tail running through a1c_result, change_flag, the diagnosis-flag dummies, the medication columns, and finally the demographic features (race, gender) and the near-zero-variance medication columns at the very bottom of the table.
Two things stand out structurally. First, no single categorical feature in this batch crosses into Cohen’s small band (V ≥ 0.10). This is the categorical equivalent of the §6 finding for continuous features — the discriminative signal is genuinely diffuse, and the modelling notebook’s job is to combine many small effects rather than ride a single dominant predictor. Second, the engineered features cluster meaningfully near the top of their respective effect bands: diag_*_group outperforms the raw diag_* codes (which are excluded from this table because of cardinality), diabetes_med_flag ties exactly with the string-form diabetes_med, and change_flag ties with change — confirming that the Gold-layer feature engineering preserves the underlying signal correctly.
One feature is conspicuously absent from this table: discharge_disposition_id, which §5.4’s separate chi-square test put at V = 0.115 (small band, the strongest categorical effect anywhere in the notebook). It is excluded from this batch because §5.4 already analysed it exhaustively with the dim-table label substitution; this batch focuses on features whose readmission association has not been tested elsewhere. The modelling notebook will use discharge_disposition_id as one of the strongest single-feature predictors available. Combined with the prior-utilisation features from §6, the modelling notebook has its top tier of signal: discharge disposition, prior inpatient visits, prior total visits, and the engineered diagnosis-group target encodings.

title: Health Analytics & Biostatistics — Exploratory Analysis of a Diabetic Inpatient Cohort
text:
8 · The HbA1c Testing Landscape
I now switch to the HbA1c cohort — one row per patient, 69,987 patients in total — to set up the causal question that notebook 03 will tackle. The clinical question is well-known in the diabetic-readmission literature: does measuring HbA1c during a diabetic admission causally reduce 30-day readmission risk? The hypothesis is that a measured A1C value gives the inpatient team better information about glycaemic control, leading to better inpatient management decisions, better discharge instructions, and ultimately lower post-discharge readmission risk.
The naive comparison — readmission rate among tested patients vs. untested patients — is straightforward to compute, but it is dominated by confounding. Patients who get tested are systematically different from patients who do not: they tend to have diabetes as a primary diagnosis, longer stays, more diagnostic activity overall. A causal estimate needs to control for those differences, and notebook 03 will do that with a doubly-robust learner. This section maps the testing landscape and runs a lightweight propensity-score logistic regression to surface the strongest confounders, so notebook 03 knows what it is up against.
The cohort schema is restricted compared to the modelling cohort: it carries only the covariates that are pre-treatment (measured before or at admission, not during the stay) plus the treatment indicator (has_hba1c_tested) and the outcome (readmitted_30d). The modelling-notebook engineering features that depend on treatment-time information are deliberately excluded.

The patient-level testing rate is 18.35% — 12,846 tested patients and 57,141 untested patients, out of 69,987 unique patients in the cohort. The 81.65% untested rate is striking for a diabetic-inpatient cohort: most patients admitted to the hospital with a diabetic comorbidity over the 2008–2009 study window did not have their HbA1c measured during the admission.
The number is the substantive starting point of the causal question. If 81.65% of admissions go untested, the question of whether testing reduces readmission risk is not just academically interesting — it is a real intervention question with policy implications. A substantial fraction of admissions could be moved from untested to tested with relatively small operational change, and the causal analysis in notebook 03 is designed to estimate the readmission-rate impact of doing so. The naive comparison in §9.1 will give a first read on the marginal effect; the propensity-adjusted estimate in notebook 03 will give the causal estimate after confounding is handled.


8.2 Testing rate by primary diagnosis

Diabetes-as-primary: tested at 35.86% (n=5,748; CI [34.63%, 37.10%]) — the highest testing rate by a wide margin, almost double the cohort average of 18.35%.
Respiratory at 19.65%, Circulatory at 19.07%, Other at 18.43% — all close to the cohort average.

The implication for the causal analysis is direct: primary diagnosis is a strong confounder of the testing decision. A patient admitted with diabetes as the primary diagnosis is both more likely to be tested (the inpatient team is actively managing glycaemic control, so they order the lab) and more likely to readmit (§5.3 showed diabetes-primary admissions had the highest per-group readmission rate at 13.10%). Without controlling for primary diagnosis, any naive testing-vs-untested comparison would conflate the effect of testing with the effect of being admitted for a diabetic event in the first place — and would likely understate or even reverse the true causal effect.
The propensity-score model in §8.4 will quantify the strength of this confounding, and notebook 03 will use the same covariate set in a doubly-robust learner to produce the adjusted estimate.


8.3 Testing rate by length of stay

The testing rate climbs monotonically with length of stay — patients who stay longer are more likely to have HbA1c measured, simply because there is more time and more opportunity for the lab order. The shortest-stay band [1, 2 days] tests at 14.99%; the longest-stay band [8, 14 days] tests at 23.56%, a 1.57× gradient across the LOS range.
This is a second strong confounder. Length of stay is associated with both the testing decision (more time → more lab orders) and the outcome (longer stays → higher readmission rate, per §5.5). The propensity-score model needs to include length of stay as a covariate, and notebook 03’s causal estimator will need to control for it.
Together, the §8.2 finding (primary-diagnosis confounding) and this section’s finding (length-of-stay confounding) define the substrate of the causal question: the testing decision is highly non-random, and a naive comparison of tested vs untested would be heavily biased. §9 below will show how biased — the stratified breakdown will reveal whether the marginal treatment effect changes sign across diagnosis strata.


8.4 Lightweight propensity-score logistic regression
I fit a small logistic regression of has_hba1c_tested on a focused set of candidate confounders, with the goal of quantifying which observed variables most strongly predict treatment assignment. This is intentionally lightweight — the full propensity model in notebook 03 will use a more extensive specification with cross-fitted regularisation. The point of fitting it here is to get a McFadden’s pseudo-R² and a coefficient table that show the substrate the causal analysis will operate on.
The covariate set follows the §8.2 and §8.3 findings: primary diagnosis group, length of stay, comorbidity load, age, demographics, prior utilisation, and a handful of admission-context features. The model is fit using statsmodels, and the cell after the inventory printout assembles the final modelling frame and calls Logit.fit().

The model converges cleanly. The summary table reports a McFadden pseudo-R² of 0.121 on 69,987 observations and 15 model degrees of freedom, with LL = −29,332 and LL-Null = −33,365 — a substantial improvement over the null model. The likelihood-ratio p-value is effectively zero, confirming that the observed covariates jointly predict treatment assignment far better than chance.
A pseudo-R² of around 0.12 is meaningful in the propensity-score context. It means the observed variables explain a substantial fraction of the variation in the testing decision — patients are not assigned to testing at random, and a model can pick up the assignment pattern using only the pre-treatment covariates available in the cohort. For the causal analysis this is good news in one direction (the propensity model has discriminative power, which is necessary for inverse-probability-weighted estimators to work) and bad news in another (the strong confounding means the naive comparison will be heavily biased).
The next cell renders the coefficient table as a forest plot, which makes the per-covariate effects easier to read than the regression table.

McFadden's pseudo-R² : 0.1209
AIC                  : 58695.6
BIC                  : 58842.0
The forest plot ranks covariates by the magnitude and direction of their effect on the testing-assignment probability, with 95% confidence intervals as horizontal bars. Several coefficients reach statistical significance, and the pattern is exactly what the §8.2 and §8.3 stratifications predicted.
The strongest positive predictors of being tested are: diabetes_med_flag (coefficient +0.375, p < 0.001) — being on a diabetic medication during admission strongly predicts having HbA1c measured; num_lab_procedures (+0.042 per procedure, p < 0.001) — admissions with more lab activity overall include more HbA1c orders; and the diag_1_group = Diabetes indicator (+0.572, the largest categorical coefficient in the table) — diabetes-as-primary admissions are far more likely to be tested. Length of stay carries a negative coefficient at −0.011 per day (p = 0.002), which is opposite to the §8.3 plot’s direction — this is a real finding worth a beat.
The apparent contradiction resolves in two ways. The univariate stratification in §8.3 shows the raw relationship between length of stay and testing rate (longer stays, more testing). The propensity-model coefficient is the partial effect of length of stay after controlling for the other covariates in the model, and the dominant covariates in the model are num_lab_procedures and diabetes_med_flag — both of which are themselves strongly correlated with length of stay. Once those two are partialled out, the residual effect of length of stay flips sign: among patients with similar lab activity and medication patterns, longer-stay patients are slightly less likely to be tested. This is a textbook confounding pattern, and surfacing it here is exactly why the propensity model exists.
Age carries a small negative coefficient at −0.017 per year (p < 0.001) — older patients are slightly less likely to be tested, after controlling for everything else. n_prior_visits_total carries a negative coefficient at −0.135 per visit (p < 0.001), which is the kind of partial-effect finding that justifies fitting a propensity model in the first place: among patients with similar clinical activity (lab procedures, medication burden, primary diagnosis), those with more prior healthcare contacts are less likely to have HbA1c measured during this admission. The plausible clinical reading is that high-utilisation patients are already managed in outpatient settings, where their HbA1c is followed between admissions, so the inpatient team does not re-order the lab. The demographic covariates (gender, race) are mostly non-significant.
Among the diagnosis-group dummies (with Circulatory as the implicit reference baseline), Digestive (−0.556), Neoplasms (−0.646), Injury (−0.406), Musculoskeletal (−0.391), and Genitourinary (−0.398) all carry strong negative coefficients — patients in those diagnosis strata are systematically less likely to be tested than patients with a circulatory primary diagnosis, consistent with the §8.2 stratification.
The takeaway for notebook 03: the propensity score is well-identified, the strongest confounders are clinical (primary diagnosis, medication, lab activity) rather than demographic, and the doubly-robust learner will need to carry these covariates carefully through the cross-fitted estimation. The naive comparison in §9 will give a first read on the marginal effect; §9.2’s stratification will preview just how much confounding moves the effect estimate.

title: Health Analytics & Biostatistics — Exploratory Analysis of a Diabetic Inpatient Cohort
text:
9 · Naive Treatment Effect & Confounding Preview
§8 established that HbA1c testing assignment is non-random and predictable from observables — the propensity-score model has a McFadden pseudo-R² of 0.121 and surfaces strong clinical confounders. Now I quantify the naive treatment effect (the unadjusted comparison of readmission rates between tested and untested patients), then preview the confounding structure by stratifying that comparison across the strongest confounders. The point of this section is not to produce the causal estimate — that’s notebook 03’s job — but to give a clear baseline that the causal estimator will be measured against, and to show how much the marginal estimate moves when even a single confounder is conditioned on.

9.1 The naive comparison
Naive treatment effect — HbA1c testing on 30-day readmission
======================================================================
Tested arm    : n = 12,846   rate =  8.40%   95% CI = [7.93%, 8.89%]
Untested arm  : n = 57,141   rate =  9.11%   95% CI = [8.88%, 9.35%]
----------------------------------------------------------------------
Naive difference : -0.71 percentage points
z-statistic      : -2.548
p-value          : 0.0108

The numbers are precise and small. The tested arm holds 12,846 patients and readmits at a rate of 8.40% (95% CI [7.93%, 8.89%]). The untested arm holds 57,141 patients and readmits at 9.11% (95% CI [8.88%, 9.35%]). The naive difference is −0.71 percentage points — patients who were tested readmit at a rate roughly 0.7 pp lower than patients who were not. The two-proportion z-test produces z = −2.55, p = 0.011 — statistically significant at the conventional α = 0.05.
The reading on this is bounded by the §8 findings. The marginal difference is in the direction clinical theory predicts (testing → better management → lower readmission), but its magnitude is small enough that the causal estimate after confounding adjustment could land anywhere from a meaningful reduction to no effect at all to (in principle) a small increase. The 95% confidence intervals on the two arm rates barely overlap, but they are not separated by much, and the 0.71 pp absolute difference would translate to a relatively small clinical impact even if it survived adjustment.
The next subsection runs the simplest possible adjustment — stratifying the comparison by primary diagnosis group — and shows how the marginal estimate behaves when even one confounder is conditioned on. The result is informative for what notebook 03 will need to build.


9.2 Stratified breakdown by a single confounder
I now stratify the tested-vs-untested comparison by primary diagnosis group — a confounder I confirmed in §8 is associated with both treatment assignment and outcome. If the stratified differences point in different directions or have wildly different magnitudes across strata, the naive marginal estimate from §9.1 is a weighted average of incompatible underlying effects, and a proper causal analysis becomes essential rather than optional.


📊 Stratified Target Rate Summary (stratum × has_hba1c_tested) — diff vs has_hba1c_tested=0

The pattern is striking and analytically important. In some diagnosis strata the tested arm has a higher readmission rate than the untested arm — and in others, the relationship reverses to the direction the marginal estimate suggests. Reading from the printed per-stratum summary, of nine evaluable strata (excluding the 3-row Missing group):

Five strata show the tested arm readmitting less than untested (the direction the marginal estimate predicts):

Injury: untested 11.29% vs tested 7.28% — −4.02 pp
Diabetes: untested 10.17% vs tested 7.23% — −2.94 pp
Respiratory: untested 7.72% vs tested 5.58% — −2.15 pp
Other: untested 9.11% vs tested 8.41% — −0.70 pp
Digestive: untested 8.09% vs tested 7.48% — −0.61 pp

Four strata show the reverse — tested readmits more:

Genitourinary: untested 8.78% vs tested 10.07% — +1.30 pp
Neoplasms: untested 8.95% vs tested 10.12% — +1.17 pp
Musculoskeletal: untested 8.30% vs tested 9.20% — +0.90 pp
Circulatory: untested 9.55% vs tested 10.20% — +0.65 pp


The marginal −0.71 pp difference from §9.1 is in technical terms a weighted average of effects that point in different directions across strata, with the weights determined by the stratum sizes. The largest negative-direction strata (Injury, Diabetes, Respiratory) together cover 19,933 of the 69,977 evaluable patients — about 28% of the cohort — while the positive-direction strata (Genitourinary, Neoplasms, Musculoskeletal, Circulatory, plus the small Other and Digestive contributions where the gap is small) cover most of the rest. The dominant strata in the cohort by patient count are Circulatory (21,389) and Other (12,124), both of which sit close to zero, which is why the marginal estimate is small even though some sub-population effects are substantial.
The clinical reading of the strata-specific patterns is informative. In the Injury and Diabetes strata — where the tested-untested gap is most negative — the tested patients may genuinely be benefiting from the test result driving better inpatient management of glycaemic control, with downstream effects on post-discharge stability. Or the gap may reflect which injury and diabetes patients get tested versus not — a selection effect that no marginal comparison can disentangle. In the Genitourinary, Neoplasms, Musculoskeletal, and Circulatory strata — where tested patients readmit at higher rates — the most likely reading is selection: the inpatient team orders HbA1c specifically when the patient looks unstable on the diabetic axis, so the tested subset within those strata is sicker to begin with.
For notebook 03 this is the substrate the doubly-robust learner needs to handle. A simple regression adjustment would assume the treatment effect is constant across strata; the data clearly violate that assumption. The DR-learner with cross-fitting allows the per-covariate-pattern treatment effect to vary, and the final estimate is a properly-weighted average across the population — which is the analytical move that will turn the noisy §9.1 marginal into a defensible causal estimate.


📊 Stratified Target Rate Summary (stratum × has_hba1c_tested) — diff vs has_hba1c_tested=0

stratum: (0.999, 2.0] | has_hba1c_tested: 1 | n: 3396 | rate_%: 6.30 | diff_vs_baseline_pp: -1.01 | 

stratum: (2.0, 3.0] | has_hba1c_tested: 0 | n: 10336 | rate_%: 8.30 | diff_vs_baseline_pp: 0.00 | 
stratum: (2.0, 3.0] | has_hba1c_tested: 1 | n: 2157 | rate_%: 7.79 | diff_vs_baseline_pp: -0.51 | 

stratum: (3.0, 6.0] | has_hba1c_tested: 0 | n: 16988 | rate_%: 9.89 | diff_vs_baseline_pp: 0.00 | 
stratum: (3.0, 6.0] | has_hba1c_tested: 1 | n: 4184 | rate_%: 8.60 | diff_vs_baseline_pp: -1.29 | 

stratum: (6.0, 14.0] | has_hba1c_tested: 0 | n: 10562 | rate_%: 11.94 | diff_vs_baseline_pp: 0.00 | 
stratum: (6.0, 14.0] | has_hba1c_tested: 1 | n: 3109 | rate_%: 10.84 | diff_vs_baseline_pp: -1.10 |
The LOS-stratified result is structurally different from the diag-stratified result. Across all four LOS quartiles, the tested arm readmits less than the untested arm — the sign is consistent:

(0.999, 2 days]: untested 7.31% vs tested 6.30% — −1.01 pp
(2, 3 days]: untested 8.30% vs tested 7.79% — −0.51 pp
(3, 6 days]: untested 9.89% vs tested 8.60% — −1.29 pp
(6, 14 days]: untested 11.94% vs tested 10.84% — −1.10 pp

The magnitude varies modestly (from −0.51 to −1.29 pp) but the direction does not flip. So unlike the diag-stratification (where the sign reverses across strata), the LOS-stratification surfaces a consistent negative gap — testing is associated with lower readmission within every length-of-stay quartile.
The marginal −0.71 pp from §9.1 is essentially a weighted average of these four quartile gaps, which all point the same direction. That is the cleaner case for a marginal estimate; it suggests the LOS confounding is dominated by level shifts (longer stays have higher overall readmission) rather than by interaction effects (testing working differently at different stay lengths).
Combining the two stratifications: confounding is real and complex. Diag-stratification surfaces direction reversal, suggesting heterogeneous treatment effects across diagnostic categories. LOS-stratification surfaces a level shift but no interaction, suggesting a more straightforward adjustment is sufficient there. A proper estimator that handles the joint covariate space is necessary to reconcile both findings into a single defensible average treatment effect — which is exactly what notebook 03’s doubly-robust learner with cross-fitting is designed to deliver.
With the causal-question substrate mapped, this notebook turns to the last two structural diagnostics: a multicollinearity scan to confirm the modelling-notebook feature set is internally well-behaved, and a CV fold integrity check that verifies the patient-disjoint split is operating as the ETL designed it to.

title: Health Analytics & Biostatistics — Exploratory Analysis of a Diabetic Inpatient Cohort
text:
10 · Multicollinearity Scan
Before I commit to a feature set for notebook 02, I check for redundancy among the continuous features. Multicollinearity inflates coefficient variance in linear models and makes individual coefficient estimates unstable, even when the model’s overall predictive power is preserved. Tree models are immune to multicollinearity in the prediction sense — they choose one of the correlated features and route the others to alternative splits — but interpretability suffers because the SHAP attributions get spread across the redundant features in unpredictable ways.
The section runs two complementary diagnostics: a Spearman correlation matrix for visual inspection of all continuous-feature pairs, and a Variance Inflation Factor (VIF) computation that quantifies multicollinearity at the feature level (rather than the pairwise level). Spearman is the right correlation choice here because several features are heavily right-skewed (the prior-utilisation counts in particular), and Pearson would be distorted by the skew.

10.1 Spearman correlation matrix

The matrix surfaces the redundancy structure I expected. age_midpoint and age_midpoint_squared are mechanically correlated — the squared term is engineered from the linear one, and their pairwise correlation lands in the moderate-to-strong band. This is by design, not a problem: linear models will use both and gain the curvature; tree models will collapse them into one and ignore the other.
The n_meds_* columns form a tight cluster of correlations. n_meds_changed, n_meds_up, n_meds_down, n_meds_steady, and n_meds_prescribed are all derived from the same underlying medication-status counts and necessarily move together. n_prior_visits_total is the sum of number_outpatient, number_emergency, and number_inpatient and is therefore mechanically correlated with all three of its components.
These are not data-quality concerns; they are arithmetic identities. The modelling notebook’s preprocessing already has a drop list that handles them — the linear model gets either the components or the aggregate (not both), and the tree models get whichever subset the SHAP analysis surfaces as most informative. The point of the matrix here is to make the redundancy structure visible before the modelling notebook’s drop list is applied, so the reader understands what is being dropped and why.
The VIF computation in the next subsection quantifies the same redundancy in a different way — a per-feature score rather than a pairwise correlation — and the two together give the full picture of the cohort’s multicollinearity landscape.

Nine features come back with VIF = inf — a numerical signal that the feature is perfectly predictable from the other features in the matrix. The takeaway for the modelling notebook is direct: the engineered redundancies are intentional and handled by the preprocessing drop list; the rest of the continuous feature space is clean. The fitted linear models will be stable, the tree models will route attention cleanly, and the SHAP analysis in notebook 02 will produce interpretable per-feature attributions.

title: Health Analytics & Biostatistics — Exploratory Analysis of a Diabetic Inpatient Cohort
text:
11 · CV Fold Sanity Check
The patient-level cross-validation split is the leakage firewall of the entire modelling phase. §6.3 of notebook 00 already confirmed structurally that the fold assignment is patient-disjoint by construction — the cv_fold column is built using GroupKFold on patient_nbr, ensuring all admissions belonging to the same patient land in the same fold. This section runs the operational verification that the modelling notebook needs before it consumes the folds: five checks across five subsections.
§11.1 verifies that the per-fold readmission rate is balanced — no fold is wildly imbalanced relative to the cohort base rate. §11.2 verifies the patient-disjoint guarantee at the row level (every patient appears in exactly one fold). §11.3 verifies that the strongest continuous predictors have stable distributions across folds, so any cross-fold variance in modelling metrics will reflect genuine model variability rather than fold-level data drift. §11.4 runs an empirical leakage check under a lean logistic-regression baseline to quantify the actual AUC inflation a row-level split would produce on this cohort. §11.5 runs the same comparison under a higher-capacity LightGBM model on the full Notebook 02 feature set, to test the same question with a model that has the capacity to memorise patient-specific patterns if the substrate exposes them.
The combination of structural verification (§11.1–§11.3) and empirical verification (§11.4–§11.5) closes the question of whether the modelling notebook can trust the pre-computed folds.

The five fold sizes are exactly equal at 19,868 admissions — the expected outcome of GroupKFold over a cohort of 99,340 admissions split into 5 folds. The target rates span a 0.33 percentage-point range from low to high, and every confidence interval overlaps every other; no fold has been dealt a systematically harder or easier class balance. This is exactly the property the modelling notebook needs: any per-fold metric variance in notebook 02 will reflect model behaviour, not accidental imbalance in the splitter’s output.


11.2 Patient-disjoint confirmation
Total unique patients in modelling cohort :  69,987
Patients appearing in more than one fold  :       0
Patient-disjoint integrity                : ✔ PASS
The integrity check is the firewall test. For each unique patient_nbr in the cohort, I count the number of distinct cv_fold values that patient appears in. Any patient with more than one fold assigned would mean the patient-disjoint guarantee is broken and any train/test evaluation would leak signal across the firewall. The output is unambiguous: of 69,987 unique patients, exactly 0 appear in more than one fold. The patient-disjoint integrity check passes.
This matters because the modelling cohort contains 99,340 admissions but only 69,987 unique patients — meaning 29.6% of admissions come from repeat patients. A naive row-level random split would put many of those patients in both train and test partitions, and any model that learned “this specific patient tends to readmit” would carry that signal directly through to the test set. Whether the leakage produces a measurable AUC inflation on this cohort depends on whether the feature set exposes patient-level idiosyncrasy that a model can memorise — §11.4 and §11.5 measure that empirically under two different model substrates. The GroupKFold over patient_nbr blocks the structural concern by construction regardless of the measured magnitude.


11.3 Feature distribution stability across folds
I check the per-fold distribution of the three strongest continuous predictors — number_inpatient, n_prior_visits_total, time_in_hospital — to confirm that no fold has been dealt a systematically different patient mix on the features that matter most for the modelling notebook. Substantial drift between folds on these features would suggest the splitter has accidentally produced easy or hard folds, even if the target rate is balanced.
